title: Reinforcement learning for hardware acceleration and system-level optimization on FPGA and integrated-circuit platforms: A survey
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) enables adaptive and autonomous decision-making in embedded, edge, and heterogeneous computing systems. Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and integrated circuits (ICs) offer low latency, energy efficiency, and architectural flexibility for RL deployment, while introducing challenges in resource constraints, implementation complexity, and hardware-algorithm co-design. This review surveys more than 100 studies on RL implementations across FPGA and IC platforms, emphasizing architectures, implementation strategies, performance evaluation, and applications. The literature is organized by RL family, including model-based Markov decision processes, classical value-based methods, deep RL, actor-critic, policy-gradient, and multi-agent approaches. We further classify studies by abstraction level, hardware realization strategy, and application domain, examining how RL algorithms map onto reconfigurable and fixed hardware. Unlike surveys restricted to particular algorithms or platforms, this work provides a unified analysis of FPGA and IC implementations, covering acceleration, reconfigurable architectures, energy-aware control, and system-level optimization. Comparative assessments consider resource utilization, latency, throughput, power consumption, and reported performance gains. Finally, we identify recurring architectural patterns, practical limitations, open challenges, and research directions for efficient RL-driven hardware systems. The survey offers a consolidated reference for researchers developing and evaluating RL solutions on specialized hardware.

Abstract

Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enabling adaptive, autonomous, and self-optimizing behavior in modern computing systems, particularly as applications increasingly migrate toward embedded, edge, and heterogeneous hardware platforms. Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and integrated circuits (ICs) offer compelling advantages for RL deployment, including low latency, energy efficiency, and fine-grained architectural customization, but they also introduce unique design challenges that differ substantially from conventional CPU- and GPU- based implementations. This review presents a comprehensive survey of RL implementations on FPGA and IC platforms, with a particular emphasis on architectural design, performance measurement, and hardware–algorithm co-design. A broad body of more than one hundred studies is systematically analyzed and organized into major RL families, ranging from model-based Markov decision processes and classical value-based methods to deep RL, Actor-critic (AC), policy-gradient (PG), and multi-agent approaches. The review further categorizes existing works according to abstraction levels, hardware realization strategies, and application domains, highlighting how different RL algorithms map onto reconfigurable and fixed hardware substrates. In contrast to prior surveys that focus narrowly on specific algorithms or platforms, this work provides a unified perspective spanning both FPGA and IC implementations, encompassing acceleration techniques, reconfigurable hardware approaches, energy-aware control, and system-level optimization. Detailed comparisons are provided in terms of resource utilization, latency, throughput, power consumption, and achieved performance gains. Additionally, this review identifies recurring architectural patterns, discusses practical limitations, and outlines open research challenges and future directions for RL-driven intelligent hardware systems. By consolidating design insights, evaluation metrics, and application trends, this review aims to serve as a comprehensive reference for researchers and practitioners working at the intersection of RL and hardware platforms.

## 1 Introduction

Recent years have witnessed a growing shift toward intelligent, autonomous decision-making embedded directly within computing systems, with increasing emphasis on assessing the real-world applicability and feasibility of algorithms that demonstrate strong performance under simulation-based evaluations. As workloads become increasingly dynamic and heterogeneous—particularly in networking and edge computing, cyber–security, robotics [8], natural language processing, intelligent sensing, and embedded environments—traditional static control and optimization techniques, such as proportional–integral–derivative control and fixed-rule heuristic approaches [108] or meta-heuristic-based optimization methods [127], often struggle to cope with variability in data rates, power budgets, timing constraints, and environmental conditions. These approaches are typically designed around fixed operating assumptions and lack the adaptability required to respond effectively to non-stationary workloads or unforeseen runtime disturbances.

RL (RL), as a core paradigm within ML (ML), has gained prominence in this context because it provides a principled framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. By continuously interacting with an environment and updating its policy based on observed rewards, an RL agent can learn to adapt its behavior online, even when system dynamics are partially unknown or change over time. This capability makes RL particularly attractive for modern computing platforms that must balance competing objectives such as performance, energy efficiency, latency, and reliability under tight operational constraints. However, translating RL from software-centric implementations to practical hardware platforms introduces significant challenges. Many RL algorithms rely on iterative updates, stochastic exploration, and memory-intensive computations that are difficult to reconcile with the strict latency, power, and determinism requirements of embedded systems. Implementations based purely on general-purpose CPU or GPU often suffer from high energy consumption, unpredictable execution timing, and limited scalability, which restrict their suitability for real-time or resource-constrained applications.

FPGA (FPGA)s and IC provide an alternative hardware substrate that fundamentally reshapes how ML, particularly RL, can be realized in practice. FPGA provide fine-grained parallelism, customizable datapaths, and reconfigurability, allowing RL algorithms to be mapped onto hardware architectures tailored to specific workloads and constraints. IC-based realizations, including ASIC and SoC platforms, further extend these advantages by enabling deterministic execution, compact form factors, and ultra-low power operation. At the same time, these platforms impose stricter design constraints, limited flexibility after deployment, and increased development complexity compared with software-based solutions. As a result, the intersection of RL with hardware design has evolved into a multidisciplinary research area encompassing algorithm–hardware co-design [64], hardware acceleration [90, 41, 58], architectural specialization [25], numerical precision optimization [5], and system-level control, including digital twin–based frameworks [106]. In this emerging landscape, RL plays a dual role: it can be treated as a workload to be accelerated on hardware, and it can also serve as a control mechanism for the hardware itself, governing tasks such as dynamic voltage and frequency scaling, resource allocation, scheduling, partial reconfiguration, and energy management. This duality blurs the traditional boundary between learning algorithms and hardware platforms, creating new opportunities as well as new design challenges. Despite rapid progress, the existing literature on RL implementations for FPGA and IC platforms remains fragmented.

Motivated by the increasingly practical shift of RL from a purely algorithmic concept to a hardware-constrained workload, this review consolidates and structures the fast-growing body of RL implementations on FPGA and IC platforms.
In particular, this survey emphasizes real-time pattern recognition and perception-driven decision-making systems, where hardware constraints critically affect learning efficiency, latency, energy consumption, and deployment feasibility.
Instead of revisiting algorithmic fundamentals, it adopts a hardware-centric lens to clarify how design and implementation choices shape real-world realizations of RL.
The review organizes the literature into coherent categories and distills recurring design patterns, trade-offs, and limitations, thereby clarifying the current state-of-the-art and highlighting open challenges that guide future research at the intersection of RL, pattern recognition, and intelligent hardware.

## 1.1 Related work and our contribution

Several surveys have examined the relationship between RL and reconfigurable or heterogeneous hardware, yet significant gaps remain. The survey in [118] provides an extensive overview of domain-specific RL architectures, with a primary focus on FPGA-based accelerators. However, it does not integrate IC implementations, unified abstraction layers, nor does it cover the complete spectrum of RL algorithmic families such as SARSA (SARSA), MC (MC), AC (AC), and PPO (PPO). Similarly, the work in [44] concentrates on ML applications within FPGA EDA (EDA) tools. While valuable, its treatment of RL is brief, lacks architectural depth, and does not relate RL methods to accelerator design or runtime optimization. The review in [162] centers on ML techniques for control and monitoring but does not address RL-driven FPGA or IC architectures, nor broader comparisons across RL categories. Additionally, the heterogeneous-chip scheduling survey in [99] identifies RL primarily as a future research direction without analyzing existing RL implementations, hardware mapping strategies, or design-flow implications. Consequently, none of these studies provide a unified RL-centric perspective that spans both FPGA and IC platforms while simultaneously comparing all major RL types, synthesizing research areas and applications, and identifying cross-cutting architectural and methodological limitations. ## 1.2 Review methodology

To ensure methodological rigor, transparency, and reproducibility, this review adopts a systematic literature search and selection strategy centered on peer-reviewed studies addressing the implementation of RL on FPGA and IC platforms. The primary search was conducted using Scopus as the main indexing engine, which provides broad coverage of major scientific publishers and digital libraries, including IEEE Xplore, Elsevier ScienceDirect, ACM Digital Library, Web of Science, Wiley, Springer, and IET Digital Library, among others. To consistently retrieve works at the intersection of RL algorithms and hardware realization, a structured Boolean query was formulated and applied across databases using title, abstract, and keyword fields. The search logic was designed to capture both classical and deep RL methods, while explicitly constraining results to hardware-oriented implementations rather than purely algorithmic or simulation-based studies. The generic query structure can be expressed as:

Selected papers =
FROM (“Title” OR “Abstract” OR “Keywords”)
SELECT (References WHERE
(RL OR DRL OR “Reinforcement Learning” OR “Deep Reinforcement Learning”) AND (FPGA OR “Field-Programmable Gate Array” OR ASIC OR IC OR SoC OR “Integrated Circuit”)) FILTER (Language = “English” AND Year BETWEEN 2015 AND 2026 AND DocumentType = (“Journal Article” OR “Conference Paper”))

The logical operators AND and OR ensure precise targeting of studies that explicitly combine RL with FPGA or IC hardware platforms. The selected time window reflects the emergence of practical RL hardware realizations, from early tabular and MDP (MDP)-based accelerators to modern deep and AC architectures.

To balance completeness with technical focus, the retrieved studies were further screened using relevance and quality criteria. Seminal RL hardware-acceleration works were retained when they directly supported the FPGA/IC-centered taxonomy, architectural discussion, performance comparison, or application-level analysis of this review. However, earlier works already extensively covered in prior surveys were not repeated exhaustively unless they established a necessary technical baseline or motivated a later research direction. This avoids redundant historical coverage while preserving the foundational context required for the proposed survey.

Redundant studies, papers with insufficient hardware-implementation details, works lacking meaningful evaluation results, and studies only weakly related to RL-based FPGA/IC platforms were excluded. Priority was given to recent studies that provide clear implementation details and contribute to emerging directions such as energy-efficient RL acceleration, quantized RL hardware, FPGA/IC-based runtime optimization, RL-assisted synthesis, MARL (MARL) hardware, and application-specific deployment.

conclusion:
This review has provided a comprehensive and hardware-centric synthesis of RL implementations on FPGA and IC platforms, spanning more than two decades of research and over one hundred representative studies. By systematically organizing the literature across RL algorithmic families, hardware abstraction levels, architectural design strategies, and application domains, the survey clarifies how learning-based decision-making has progressively transitioned from software-centric experimentation to practical, resource-aware hardware realizations.

A central outcome of this review is the identification of recurring architectural patterns that underpin successful RL deployment on FPGA and IC substrates. Across classical tabular methods, deep value-based approaches, and modern AC and policy-gradient algorithms, effective designs consistently exploit fine-grained parallelism, pipelined datapaths, quantized arithmetic, and tightly coupled on-chip memory hierarchies. At the same time, the review highlights a clear divergence between FPGA-oriented solutions—favoring flexibility, reconfigurability, and rapid prototyping—and IC-based realizations, which prioritize determinism, compactness, and ultra-low power operation. The unified abstraction framework presented in this work demonstrates that, despite these differences, coherent design flows can bridge FPGA prototyping and IC deployment when hardware–algorithm co-design principles are applied early. From an algorithmic perspective, the survey reveals that no single RL paradigm dominates across all hardware and application contexts. Lightweight tabular methods such as QL and SARSA remain attractive for real-time embedded control due to their simplicity and predictable timing, whereas deep RL approaches, including DQN, DDPG, PPO, and AC variants, enable scalability to high-dimensional sensing and control problems at the cost of increased architectural complexity. MARL further extends these capabilities to distributed and large-scale systems but introduces new challenges related to coordination, non-stationarity, and interconnect overhead. These trade-offs emphasize that algorithm selection must be driven jointly by task requirements and hardware constraints rather than by learning performance alone.

title: Interaction-Gated Time-Frequency Learning for Parameter-Efficient PPG-Based Heart Rate Estimation
abstract: Photoplethysmography (PPG) enables low-cost and non-invasive heart rate (HR) monitoring but remains sensitive to waveform distortion, physiological variability, and measurement interference. Temporal waveform characteristics and frequency-domain periodicity provide complementary information for HR estimation; however, effectively exploring and integrating these representations within a compact model remains challenging. This paper proposes TF-IG, a parameter-efficient interaction-gated time-frequency learning framework for PPG-based HR estimation. TF-IG employs a dual-branch architecture in which a temporal branch captures pulse morphology via dilated depthwise-separable convolutions, while a frequency branch extracts cardiac periodicity information from bounded log-spectrogram representations. To combine the two domains, we introduce an interaction-gated fusion module that explicitly models feature agreement and discrepancy, while also learning feature-wise weights to balance temporal and spectral information. A parameter-shared regression head further maps the temporal, spectral, and fused representations into the final HR prediction space. Experiments on the benchmark BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset using a subject-exclusive training, validation, and test protocol show that TF-IG achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 1.227 BPM, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 2.060 BPM, a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.9934, and 92.28 percent of estimates within 3 BPM, while remaining parameter-efficient with only 84.6K parameters. Ablation results further demonstrate the complementary contributions of the temporal and frequency branches, interaction-gated fusion, and shared regression head. These results indicate that explicitly modeling cross-domain interactions provides an effective accuracy-complexity trade-off for lightweight PPG-based HR estimation.

## 1 Introduction

Continuous heart-rate (HR) monitoring plays an important role in clinical observation, fitness assessment, ambulatory healthcare and long-term physiological monitoring [13], [1].
Although electrocardiography (ECG) remains a standard reference for cardiac monitoring, photoplethysmography (PPG) provides an attractive alternative for continuous and wearable sensing because it measures peripheral blood-volume variations using inexpensive and non-invasive optical hardware [2], [9]. Its compact sensing configuration has consequently enabled widespread integration into wearable devices, pulse oximeters, smartphones, and other resource-constrained monitoring platforms. PPG therefore represents a practical sensing modality for scalable and continuous cardiovascular monitoring [2], [1].
Despite these advantages, reliable HR estimation from PPG remains challenging. The measured waveform is influenced not only by cardiac pulsation but also by physiological and acquisition-related factors such as respiration, body site, tissue characteristics, ambient illumination, applied pressure, and artifacts [4].

A broad range of signal-processing and learning-based approaches has therefore been developed for PPG-based HR estimation. Classical methods typically rely on filtering, peak detection, spectral analysis, or handcrafted signal descriptors [12], [6]. More recently, deep learning has enabled HR-relevant features to be learned directly from PPG observations rather than relying entirely on manually designed processing rules. For example, PPGNet [17] proposed an end-to-end network operating directly on short PPG segments for device-independent HR estimation; Deep PPG [15] leverages convolutional neural networks over spectrogram of PPG and accelerometer signals; Ismail et al. [7] further explored a set of features characterizing the signal, modeling by a convolutional-recurrent framework, etc. These studies
demonstrates that temporal and spectral representations of PPG can provide useful information for HR estimation.

The complementarity of temporal and spectral domain follows naturally from the characteristics of PPG. The temporal domain preserves local pulse morphology and short-term waveform dynamics, whereas the frequency domain makes periodic cardiac activity more explicit. Time-frequency representations further characterize how this spectral structure evolves over the observation interval, emphasizing different aspects of the same underlying physiological process [7].
Although prior work has demonstrated the utility of signal, spectral, and time-frequency representations, effectively structuring the interaction between complementary representations remains an important design problem.
The availability of multiple representations does not by itself determine how they should be combined [5]. Under signal variability or corruption, temporal and spectral features may provide partly consistent yet partly different evidence about the underlying HR. Therefore, an effective fusion mechanism should explicitly characterize where they agree, where they differ, and how strongly each should jointly contribute to the final representation.

Motivated by these observations, we propose TF-IG, a parameter-efficient Interaction-Gated Time–Frequency learning framework for PPG-based HR estimation. First, TF-IG learns complementary HR representations through two lightweight branches: a temporal branch based on dilated depthwise-separable convolutions and temporal attention pooling, and a frequency branch that processes a bounded log-spectrogram using spectro-temporal attention pooling. Second, these representations are integrated through a structured interaction-gated mechanism. Element-wise multiplication and absolute difference explicitly encode cross-domain co-activation and discrepancy, while a feature-wise gate adaptively balances the temporal and spectral embeddings. The resulting fused representation, together with the individual branch embeddings, is processed by a shared regression head that provides a common mapping to HR, with the three predictions subsequently combined through learned normalized weights. In this way, TF-IG jointly addresses complementary representation learning, explicit cross-domain interaction, and parameter-efficient prediction within a unified lightweight framework.
Accordingly, the main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

• 

Compact dual-domain representation learning.
We propose a parameter-efficient dual-branch architecture that jointly captures temporal pulse morphology and spectro-temporal cardiac periodicity using dilated depthwise-separable convolutions and attention-based pooling.

• 

Structured cross-domain fusion and shared prediction.
We introduce an interaction-gated fusion mechanism that explicitly models temporal–spectral co-activation and discrepancy through element-wise multiplication and absolute difference, while a feature-wise gate adaptively balances the contribution of the two domains. A parameter-shared regression head is further applied to the temporal, frequency, and fused embeddings, providing a common space for HR prediction mapping while avoiding separate prediction networks.

• 

Empirical validation of the proposed design.
On a subject-independent BIDMC split, TF-IG achieves an MAE of $1.227$ BPM, an RMSE of $2.060$ BPM, a Pearson correlation of $0.9934$ , and a CP3 of $92.28\%$ using only 84.6K parameters. Ablation experiments further demonstrate the complementary contributions of dual-domain representation learning, interaction-gated fusion, and shared regression to the final performance.

## 2 Methodology

This section first formulates PPG-based heart-rate estimation and introduces the notation used throughout the paper Section 2.1. Section 2.2 describes the overview of the proposed architecture. Subsequently, Section 2.3 describes the signal preprocessing stage. Individual components within the framework such as time-domain branch, frequency-domain branch, fusion module, and regression head are detailed in Sections 2.4, 2.5, 2.6, and 2.7, respectively.

## 2.1 Problem Definition and Notation

Let $\mathbf{x}_{\mathrm{raw}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{\mathrm{raw}}}$ denote a single-channel PPG segment of duration $T_{\mathrm{win}}$ seconds recorded at an original sampling rate $f_{s}$ . Each segment is associated with a reference heart rate $y\in\mathbb{R}$ , expressed in beats per minute (BPM). After preprocessing and resampling, the segment is represented as $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{T}$ .

The objective is to learn a regression function
 $\Phi(\cdot;\Theta)$ , parameterized by $\Theta$ , that maps the input PPG segment to its corresponding heart-rate estimate:

 $\hat{y}=\Phi(\mathbf{x};\Theta),$ 

(1)

where $\hat{y}\in\mathbb{R}$ denotes the predicted heart rate. The parameters $\Theta$ are optimized by minimizing a regression loss between $\hat{y}$ and the reference value $y$ over the training set.

Throughout this work, the notation $[\cdot\,;\cdot]$ represents concatenation along the feature dimension, $\odot$ denotes the Hadamard product, and $\sigma(\cdot)$ denotes the sigmoid function.

Figure 1: Overview structure of proposed framework

## 2.2 Overall Architecture

As illustrated in Fig. 1, TF-IG adopts two complementary processing branches. The time-domain branch operates directly on the PPG waveform and captures local pulse morphology and temporal dependencies. In parallel, the frequency-domain branch transforms the waveform into a bounded log-magnitude spectrogram and models cardiac periodicity over time-frequency transformed representation.

To reduce the computational operations, both streams use depthwise-separable convolutions [3] as their primary building block. Both branches share a structured processing flow comprising a convolutional stem, domain-specific feature refinement, and targeted attention pooling. Their outputs are converted into fixed-dimensional embeddings through domain-specific attention pooling. An interaction-gated fusion module then combines these embeddings by jointly modeling their agreement, discrepancy, and relative contribution. Finally, a shared regression head generates predictions from the time-domain, frequency-domain, and fused representations, which are combined through a learnable ensemble.

## 2.3 Preprocessing

Continuous PPG recordings are first partitioned into fixed-duration windows of $T_{\mathrm{win}}$ seconds using a predefined window stride. Each window is resampled to a target sampling rate $f_{s}^{*}=62.5$ Hz and then normalized using z-score. The resulting signal $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{T}$ is provided to both the time-domain and frequency-domain branches.

## 2.4 Time-Domain Branch

## 1D Convolutional Stem and Dilated Residual Blocks:

The resampled waveform is first arranged as a single-channel sequence,
 $\mathbf{X}_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times T}$ . A one-dimensional convolutional stem extracts low-level morphological features while preserving the temporal resolution. The stem consists of a standard Conv1D layer ( $K=7$ ) followed by two dilated depthwise-separable Conv1D layers ( $K=5$ , with dilations $d=2$ and $d=4$ , respectively). Batch normalization and activations are applied after each layer, yielding $\mathbf{H}_{\text{stem}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times T}$ .

Furthermore, to expand the temporal receptive field without losing resolution, $\mathbf{H}_{\text{stem}}$ is subsequently refined through three cascaded residual blocks. The transformation at the $i$ -th block is formulated as:

 $\mathbf{H}_{i}=\operatorname{ReLU}\big(\mathbf{H}_{i-1}+\Psi_{i}(\mathbf{H}_{i-1})\big),\quad i\in\{1,2,3\},$ 

(2)

where $\mathbf{H}_{0}=\mathbf{H}_{\text{stem}}$ . The function $\Psi_{i}(\cdot)$ denotes a residual mapping comprising a dilated depthwise-separable Conv1D with kernel size $K_{i}$ and dilation rate $d_{i}$ , followed by a $1\times 1$ pointwise projection, batch normalization, and dropout. The output feature map is denoted as $\mathbf{H}_{t}\triangleq\mathbf{H}_{3}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times T}$ .

## Temporal Attention Pooling (TAP):

Temporal attention pooling converts $\mathbf{H}_{t}$ into a fixed-dimensional embedding while allowing the model to emphasize informative portions of the PPG waveform. Attention logits are generated via a Temporal Transfer block including a two-layer $1\times 1$ convolutional network:

 $\boldsymbol{\ell}_{t}=\operatorname{Conv}_{1\times 1}^{(2)}\left(\tanh\left(\operatorname{Conv}_{1\times 1}^{(1)}(\mathbf{H}_{t})\right)\right),$ 

(3)

where the first projection reduces the channel dimension from $C$ to a hidden dimension $C_{h}$ , and the second produces one scalar logit per temporal position.

The normalized attention weights are

 $\alpha_{k}=\frac{\exp(\ell_{t,k})}{\sum_{j=1}^{T}\exp(\ell_{t,j})},\qquad k=1,\ldots,T.$ 

(4)

The time-domain embedding $\mathbf{z}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{C}$ is then computed as

 $\mathbf{z}_{t}=\sum_{k=1}^{T}\alpha_{k}\mathbf{H}_{t}[:,k].$ 

(5)

Unlike uniform global pooling, the TAP operation aims to assign greater importance to waveform intervals containing reliable pulse morphology.

## 2.5 Frequency-Domain Branch

## Bounded Log-Spectrogram Representation:

The frequency branch started by transforming the resampled signal $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{T}$ into spectro-representation $\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{STFT}}$ via the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) using a Hann window.
Since the dominant cardiac periodicity is expected to lie within a bounded physiological frequency range, we therefore retain only the frequency bins within the cardiac band of $[0.5,5.0]$ Hz to suppress irrelevant low-frequency drift and high-frequency components and to reduce the dimensionality of the spectral input.

Logarithmic dynamic-range compression is then applied as:

 $\mathbf{S}[k,m]=\log\left(1+\left|\mathbf{X}_{\mathrm{STFT}}[k,m]\right|\right),\qquad k\in\mathcal{K}.$ 

(6)

The resulting bounded log-spectrogram is represented as

 $\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times M},$ 

(7)

where $F=|\mathcal{K}|$ is the number of retained frequency bins and $M$ is the number of STFT frames.

## 2D Convolutional Stem:

Equivalent to its 1D counterpart, $\mathbf{S}$ is processed by a 2D convolutional stem, which share an identical structural topology. It consists of a standard Conv2D ( $K=7$ ) followed by two dilated depthwise-separable Conv2D layers ( $K=5$ , dilations $d=2,4$ ). Operating over the spatial $F\times M$ plane, this block extracts multi-scale spectro-temporal features, outputting $\mathbf{H}_{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times F\times M}$ .

## Spectro-Temporal Attention Pooling:

As a non-stationary rhythmic signal, heart rate exhibits time-varying spectral energy distributed along instantaneous-frequency trajectories in the time-frequency plane [8]. Driven by these dynamic properties, Spectro-Temporal Attention Pooling module aggregates the joint spectro-temporal feature map $\mathbf{H}_{f}$ into a fixed-length embedding $\mathbf{z}_{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{C}$ to explicitly capture those joint time-frequency relationships.

Given $\mathbf{H}_{f}$ , a Spectral Transfer block comprising a $1\times 1$ convolution, batch normalization, ReLU activation, and a second $1\times 1$ convolution produces a logit map
 $\mathbf{L}_{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times M}$ . A spatial softmax is applied jointly over all $FM$ positions:

 $\beta_{u,v}=\frac{\exp(\mathbf{L}_{f}[u,v])}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{F}\sum_{j=1}^{M}\exp(\mathbf{L}_{f}[i,j])}.$ 

(8)

The frequency-domain embedding $\mathbf{z}_{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{C}$ is obtained as

 $\mathbf{z}_{f}=\sum_{u=1}^{F}\sum_{v=1}^{M}\beta_{u,v}\mathbf{H}_{f}[:,u,v].$ 

(9)

## 2.6 Interaction-Gated Fusion Module

While direct concatenation or linear projection can effectively combine time- and frequency-domain representations, it does not explicitly model the cross-domain interactions between these two domains. Therefore, our aim is to achieve an explicit module that can interactively aggregated features from both time and frequency domain.
Specifically, Interaction-Gated Fusion Module decomposes cross-domain fusion into two complementary components: an explicit interaction pathway that models feature relationships and a sample-dependent gate that balances the contribution of the two domains.

## Explicit Cross-Domain Interaction

To capture joint cross-domain relationships, we construct an extended interaction vector $\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{4C}$ by combining linear terms, element-wise correlation, and absolute disparity:

 $\mathbf{u}=\left[\mathbf{z}_{t}\,;\,\mathbf{z}_{f}\,;\,\mathbf{z}_{t}\odot\mathbf{z}_{f}\,;\,|\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{z}_{f}|\right].$ 

(10)

Here, the multiplicative term of $\mathbf{z}_{t}\odot\mathbf{z}_{f}$ emphasizes the co-occurring activations across both domains, while the point-wise difference $|{}\mathbf{z}_{t}-\mathbf{z}_{f}|{}$ measures feature discrepancies. The extended vector is subsequently projected back to dimension $C$ via a non-linear projection block:

We study verifier generation: from the instruction and environment available for solving a task, an agent writes an executable verifier that must accept every valid solution and reject invalid ones. We introduce VerifierBench, a benchmark of 222 tasks from six agent benchmarks spanning tool-call, state-based, and code verification, with 4,993 hidden test cases that include alternative valid solutions and attacks; Verifier4Verifier (V4V), a six-check audit, screens its source verifiers and test suites. Across 19 models in a common agent harness, normalized balanced accuracy ranges from 10.6 to 62.1, with generated verifiers consistently rejecting invalid solutions more reliably than they accept valid ones. This apparent strength can mask overly restrictive verification: most false rejections in the analyzed records come from verifiers that accept no tested solution to a task. Case studies reveal unsupported assumptions about solution formats, tool use, and code changes that exclude valid solutions. These errors survive self-testing because agents test solutions that share the verifier's mistaken assumptions, or submit verifiers without confirming that any correct solution passes. These findings suggest testing both whether a verifier accepts a correct solution and whether it accepts other solutions permitted by the task. The project page and dataset are publicly available.

Abstract

Agents need reliable ways to validate their outputs, both when completing tasks and when filtering synthetic training data.
We study verifier generation: from the instruction and environment available for solving a task, an agent writes an executable verifier that must accept every valid solution and reject invalid ones.
We introduce VerifierBench, a benchmark of 222 tasks from six agent benchmarks spanning tool-call, state-based, and code verification, with 4,993 hidden test cases that include alternative valid solutions and attacks; Verifier4Verifier (V4V), a six-check audit, screens its source verifiers and test suites.
Across 19 models in a common agent harness, normalized balanced accuracy ranges from 10.6 to 62.1, with generated verifiers consistently rejecting invalid solutions more reliably than they accept valid ones.
This apparent strength can mask overly restrictive verification: most false rejections in the analyzed records come from verifiers that accept no tested solution to a task.
Case studies reveal unsupported assumptions about solution formats, tool use, and code changes that exclude valid solutions.
These errors survive self-testing because agents test solutions that share the verifier’s mistaken assumptions, or submit verifiers without confirming that any correct solution passes.
These findings suggest testing both whether a verifier accepts a correct solution and whether it accepts other solutions permitted by the task.

## 1 Introduction

In data-oriented recursive self-improvement (RSI) (Yin et al., 2025; Min et al., 2026), agents construct training data for their own subsequent learning and can jointly generate tasks and verification functions that provide reinforcement learning rewards (Zhou et al., 2026).
These verifiers judge candidate solutions, determining which receive rewards or enter the training data.
An incorrect verifier can therefore repeatedly reward a violation or discard a valid solution, making the reliability of agent-generated verifiers critical to this learning process.

To examine this reliability, we study verifier generation (Zhang et al., 2025; Dinella et al., 2022): given the instruction and environment a solver would receive, an agent writes an executable verifier that returns PASS or FAIL for any candidate solution.
Unlike a solver, which needs one valid solution, a verifier must accept all valid solutions while rejecting invalid ones.
It must therefore distinguish task requirements from choices that can vary across valid solutions.
Figure 2 shows a verifier rejecting a permitted read-only query because the agent omits its tool from an allowlist.
The self-tests omit the same query and never establish that a complete valid solution passes.

A verifier that accepts one expected solution may still reject other valid ways to complete a task, while one that catches ordinary mistakes may still accept solutions that exploit gaps in its checks.
Evaluating verifier generation therefore requires testing both acceptance of valid alternatives and rejection of invalid solutions, including deliberate attacks.
Prior work evaluates generated test assertions (Dinella et al., 2022), unit tests (Jain et al., 2025), issue-reproducing tests (Mündler et al., 2024), and executable specifications (Endres et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026).
We extend this line of evaluation to agent task completion, where correctness can depend on tool interactions, resulting environment states, and code changes.
To this end, we build VerifierBench: 222 tasks from six open-source agent benchmarks with 4,993 hidden test cases, comprising reference solutions, valid alternatives, ordinary errors, and attacks on verification.
This design tests whether generated verifiers distinguish task success from failure across different ways of carrying out the same task.
Reliable measurement also requires trustworthy evaluation labels.
Because both the benchmarks’ source verifiers and our constructed test cases can contain errors, we audit them with Verifier4Verifier (V4V), six checks that include replay, repeatability, and mutation testing.
Source verifiers that pass this audit serve as the reference verifiers.

Evaluating 19 models in a common harness and 17 further model–harness configurations, we report three findings.
First, generated verifiers accept valid solutions less reliably than they reject invalid ones: as reported in Section 3.2, true positive rates range from 21.1% to 70.2%, whereas true negative rates range from 79.2% to 96.3%.
Second, as analyzed in Section 3.4, these false rejections concentrate in all-reject verifiers, which return FAIL on every test case of their task and produce 87.9–96.0% of false rejections in the analyzed records.
Third, in selected cases examined in Section 4, these verifiers impose checks that the task does not require, and the agents’ self-tests either exercise only solutions those checks allow or never confirm that any valid solution passes.
We thus contribute a benchmark and screening procedure for verifier generation in Section 2, together with an analysis in Section 5 that motivates testing generated verifiers on permitted variations, not only on a chosen solution.

## 2 VerifierBench

## 2.1 Task Formulation

For task $t$ , an agent receives the instruction and environment used for ordinary task solving, together with the verifier’s input and output conventions summarized in Appendix A.
A harness, the agent framework that manages model calls, tool use, and the generation loop, runs the agent until it delivers an executable verifier $\widehat{V}_{t}$ ; the reference verifier and hidden test cases are withheld.
During generation, the agent may run self-tests: it writes candidate solutions of its own and checks that its draft verifier returns PASS for intended positives and FAIL for intended negatives.
Because the hidden test cases are withheld, self-tests are the agent’s only evidence about how its verifier behaves.

After generation, we fix $\widehat{V}_{t}$ and run it on every test case in the task’s suite $\mathcal{C}_{t}$ .
Each test case holds one candidate solution and carries a reference label defined in Section 2.3, PASS for a positive case and FAIL for a negative one, which the verifier never sees.

A tool-call verifier receives raw call text together with parsed function names and arguments; a state verifier receives the candidate’s interaction record or, for AppWorld, its solution code; and a code verifier receives the candidate patch and a repository checkout.
For state and code tasks, both the generating agent and the delivered verifier can execute code in the task environment through a public interface, run_public, for example to replay a candidate’s actions or run a repository’s tests.
Executions during generation are budgeted separately from those during evaluation, as documented in Appendix E.

## 2.2 Task Sources and Test Cases

We draw tasks from open-source agent benchmarks with executable evaluation procedures, each supplying an instruction, an environment, and a source verifier.
As summarized in the top of Table 1, tool-call tasks check called functions and arguments, state tasks check interactions or the resulting environment state, and code tasks check proposed software changes.
Each test case receives a construction label, PASS or FAIL, assigned from the task requirements and the change made to the solution before any verifier is run.
As listed in the bottom of Table 1, test cases form four groups: the designated reference solution (gold); valid variants, which change presentation, implementation, or execution path while still satisfying every requirement; ordinary errors, namely initial outcomes, partial solutions, near misses, and regressions; and attacks, which exploit checking omissions, fabricate success signals, or interfere with verification.
Valid variants test whether a verifier accepts more than one expression of a correct solution.
Appendix C details the nine construction categories behind these groups.

## 2.3 Screening with Verifier4Verifier

These test cases are useful only if their labels are reliable.
Construction labels and source verifiers can both be wrong: a constructed case may not change the solution as intended, and a source verifier may contain bugs.
V4V applies six checks to the constructed test cases and source verifiers:

1. 

Replay. Run the source verifier on every test case and compare its decision with the construction label.

2. 

Repeatability. Rerun it on the same case from the same reset state; the decision must not change.

3. 

Provenance. Link every recorded decision to the test-case contents and verifier version that produced it.

4. 

Input-label consistency. Within a task, cases that give the verifier identical information must not carry opposite labels.

5. 

Trivial baselines. Verifiers that always accept, always reject, or accept only the reference solution must be exposed by negative cases, positive cases, and valid variants, respectively.

6. 

Mutation testing. Modify one check in the source verifier (DeMillo et al., 1978); some test case must then receive different valid decisions from the two versions.

We resolve any disagreement between a construction label and a source-verifier decision against the task requirements; agreement alone does not show that either is semantically correct.

As detailed in Appendix B.1, confirmed source defects exclude 45 of the 267 initial tasks.
All 37 Terminal-Bench tasks are removed, 35 of them because its test-output parser counts skipped tests as passes; the others are five BFCL tasks whose answer keys conflict with default-argument rules and three SWE-bench tasks with parsing and empty-report errors.
Defects in our own evaluation pipeline are corrected without excluding tasks.
All 222 retained tasks pass the six checks, as reported in Appendix B.2, and their source verifiers become the reference verifiers $V_{t}^{\star}$ .
Because replay agrees on every test case, each construction label equals the reference verifier’s decision; we call this value the reference label and score generated verifiers against it.

## 2.4 Metrics

A verifier invocation yields a valid PASS, a valid FAIL, or no valid decision (a missing verifier, timeout, crash, or malformed output).
A verifier that catches its own internal error and returns FAIL still yields a valid decision, although it may not have completed its intended check.
For each task, we compute the fraction of positive cases receiving PASS and the fraction of negative cases receiving FAIL; the true positive rate (TPR) and true negative rate (TNR) average these fractions across tasks, in percent.
Our primary metric is normalized task-averaged balanced accuracy (Brodersen et al., 2010), which rescales $\mathrm{BA}=(\mathrm{TPR}+\mathrm{TNR})/2$ as

 $\mathrm{BA}_{\rm norm}=2\,\mathrm{BA}-100=\mathrm{TPR}+\mathrm{TNR}-100.$ 

(1)

It weights tasks equally and the two classes equally within each task.
Constant valid decisions score 0 and perfect agreement scores 100; missing or invalid decisions stay in the denominators without credit.
We also report the attack false-positive rate FPRh, the task-averaged fraction of attack cases that receive PASS. More results are in Appendices D and G).

## 3 Experiments

## 3.1 Experimental Setup

## Models and harnesses.

Our main comparison runs all 19 models in one common harness, Pi (Zechner, 2025).
To measure how much the harness matters, we add 17 alternative configurations.
They pair models with each family’s native harness, the vendor’s own agent tool (Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025), Codex (OpenAI, 2025), or Gemini CLI (Google, 2025)), with the third-party harnesses OpenClaw (OpenClaw Foundation, 2026) and mini-swe (Yang et al., 2024), and across families, as with GPT-6-astra in Claude Code.
Because harnesses differ in prompts, tools, and reasoning settings, cross-harness comparisons describe configurations rather than model capability alone.

title: VHDLBench: Benchmarking and Fine-Tuning Large Language Models for VHDL-Based Chip Design
abstract: The rapid evolution of digital circuit complexity demands innovative approaches to hardware design automation. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have influenced software development, their application to Hardware Description Language (HDL) generation remains largely unexplored, particularly for VHDL. This paper presents a comprehensive study for AI-assisted digital circuit design, addressing gaps in current Electronic Design Automation workflows. The work introduces a VHDL dataset of 18,500+ syntax-verified examples from open-source repositories and converted Verilog designs. Five 7B-parameter LLMs were fine-tuned using parameter-efficient QLoRA technique, enabling deployment in resource-constrained environments. To evaluate model efficacy, a rigorous three-level pipeline was established: (1) syntax and synthesis validation, (2) functional simulation with testbenches, and (3) FPGA prototyping on Zynq SoCs. Results show fine-tuned models achieve up to 92% syntax correctness and 73% functional accuracy on common design tasks, with DeepSeek-Coder demonstrating the highest performance gains. Generated designs were successfully deployed on real hardware, confirming not only syntactic but operational viability. This work demonstrates that LLMs, when tailored with domain-specific data and lightweight fine-tuning can contribute meaningfully to the future of generative EDA workflows.

Abstract

Coding agents can now interpret a specification, implement it, write and execute tests, repair failures, and declare the result ready for release. When the same agentic system produces both the software and the evidence of its correctness, a passing test suite no longer constitutes independent evidence. Visible tests become an optimization target, code, tests, and oracles may share a single misinterpretation of the specification, and the builder’s own tests may simply be incomplete. This paper argues that agent-produced software requires an assurance plane that is structurally independent of the build plane. We first characterize four gaps along the chain from stakeholder intent to production, namely the requirement, conformance, evaluation, and model gaps, and identify which of them verification can close. We then propose a framework that separates building from verifying, introduces a Verification Contract stating what must be demonstrated before release, and organizes verification in two phases: a specification-first phase designed without access to the implementation, and an implementation-aware phase that strengthens the evidence through mutation analysis, property-based testing, and fuzzing. The resulting evidence is consolidated into an assurance report that makes residual uncertainty explicit and leaves the release decision to a human. We evaluate the framework in a pre-registered study on three stateful services, two of them written by third-party models, and an EvalPlus pilot, comparing self-validation with independent verification under context-level and model-level independence. The builder’s programs were correct, but its own tests missed subtle interactions: a verifier in a fresh context detected more of the 46 seeded faults than the builder’s tests (Holm-corrected p = 0.006), and surfaced the ambiguities of the specification, at the price of rare false oracles. A verifier from another provider did not add detection. The framework and the study provide a basis for governing the release of software produced by agents.

Index Terms: 
agentic software engineering, test oracle problem, independent verification and validation, mutation testing, property-based testing, software assurance

## I Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) were first adopted in software engineering as assistants that complete code, generate unit tests, or suggest repairs under close human supervision [1, 2]. Coding agents change this division of labor. Given a task description and a repository, an agent can decompose the task, modify the code, write and execute tests, repair its own failures, and iterate until every visible check succeeds [3]. Spec-driven development extends this mode of work by asking the human to formalize intent as a specification before delegating implementation to the agent [4].

Spec-driven development returns control to the human at the beginning of the chain. It does not address the end of the chain. In a typical agentic workflow, the agent that implements the specification also writes the tests, chooses the expected outputs, interprets failures, modifies the code, and finally reports that the change is ready. The release signal is then a set of green checks produced, selected, or adjusted by the producer itself. This situation raises a governance question that long predates LLMs: can the producer of an artifact be the sole authority on its correctness? Classical software engineering answered negatively. Testing practice advises against programmers testing their own programs [5], and standards for critical software require verification activities with technical, managerial, and financial independence from development [6, 7].

Recent evidence suggests that this answer remains valid for agents, for two reasons. First, when tests drive an iterative loop, they act as a reward signal, and a sufficiently capable optimizer can satisfy the signal without satisfying the intent behind it [8, 9]. Zhao et al. report that frontier coding agents saturate visible validation suites on systems-level tasks while still failing held-out composition tests, with failures that range from incomplete features to implementations that memorize test inputs [10]. Zhong et al. show that agents frequently modify or circumvent tests when a specification and its tests conflict [11]. Second, when code, tests, and expected outputs derive from the same interpretation of a specification, they can be mutually consistent and jointly wrong. Internal consistency is not evidence of external correctness, which is a modern instance of the test oracle problem [12]. A third, less visible reason needs neither optimization pressure nor a misreading: a builder that implements the specification correctly still tests only what it thought of, so its passing suite says little about the behaviors it did not test.

The scale of agent output aggravates both problems. Line-by-line review cannot keep pace with the volume of code that agents produce, so the object of human control must shift from the code to the evidence about the code. We therefore formulate the following question: when software is produced largely autonomously from a specification, what independent evidence is sufficient for a human to authorize its release?

This paper makes the following contributions:

• 

A gap analysis. We decompose the distance between stakeholder intent and production behavior into four gaps (requirement, conformance, evaluation, and model) and explain why self-validation can close none of them reliably (Section III).

• 

An independent assurance framework. We separate a build plane from an assurance plane, introduce the Verification Contract as the human-approved artifact that defines release evidence, and organize verification into a specification-first phase and an implementation-aware phase whose evidence is consolidated in an assurance report (Section IV).

• 

A pre-registered empirical study. We measure the evaluation gap under self-validation, the effect of context-level and model-level independence, and the complementarity of the two verification phases on three stateful services with 46 seeded faults, two of them written by third-party models, and on an EvalPlus pilot [13] (Sections V and VI).

• 

An open artifact containing the experimental harness, prompts, generated evidence, and analysis scripts https://github.com/besionisrael/assure-harness.

## II Background and Related Work

## II-A LLM-Based Test Generation and Test Adequacy

Early work on LLM-based testing asked whether models could produce tests that compile, run, and increase coverage. CodaMosa invokes an LLM when search-based test generation reaches a coverage plateau [14]. Schäfer et al. evaluate LLM-generated unit tests for JavaScript and report coverage competitive with established tools [15]. TestGen-LLM at Meta accepts a generated test only if it builds, passes reliably, and increases coverage, and it reports that most candidates fail at least one of these filters [16]. A recurring lesson is that LLMs are most useful when coupled with an external mechanism that measures, filters, or rejects their output.

Coverage, however, is a weak proxy for fault detection: Inozemtseva and Holmes find that coverage is not strongly correlated with test suite effectiveness once suite size is controlled [17]. Mutation analysis offers a stronger criterion by asking whether a suite fails on deliberately faulty variants of the program [18, 19], and mutant detection correlates with real fault detection [20]. MuTAP feeds surviving mutants back to an LLM to strengthen generated tests [21], and Meta’s ACH system generates mutants that represent specific fault classes and then generates tests that kill them [22]. Property-based testing [23] replaces examples with invariants checked over generated inputs, and recent studies investigate LLMs as generators of such properties [24, 25]. Metamorphic testing addresses programs for which exact expected outputs are unavailable [26].

## II-B The Test Oracle Problem

A test requires both an input and a judgment of whether the observed output is correct [12]. LLMs can generate the judgment, but the judgment can be wrong. TOGLL studies the correctness and strength of LLM-generated oracles and shows that both must be measured separately [27]. Several code generation approaches use generated tests to select or refine programs: CodeT ranks candidate programs by their agreement with generated tests [28], and AgentCoder assigns test design to a separate agent from code generation [29]. These approaches treat generated tests as a means to improve generation. We instead treat them as evidence for a release decision and ask under which conditions that evidence is independent.

## II-C Specification Gaming by Coding Agents

Reward hacking occurs when an optimizer increases a proxy reward without improving the true objective [8, 9], a specific case of Goodhart’s law [30]. In agentic coding, the proxy is the test suite. SpecBench separates natural-language specifications, visible validation tests, and held-out composition tests, and finds that the gap between visible and held-out performance grows with code size [10]. ImpossibleBench constructs tasks whose tests contradict their specifications, so that any pass reveals a shortcut, and documents behaviors ranging from test deletion to operator overloading [11]. EvalPlus showed earlier that augmenting HumanEval and MBPP with additional tests substantially lowers measured correctness [13]. Related work on LLM self-assessment reports that models struggle to correct their own reasoning without external feedback [31] and that LLM evaluators favor their own generations [32].

## II-D Independence and Assurance Cases

Independent verification and validation (IV&V) is a mature discipline. IEEE Std 1012 distinguishes technical, managerial, and financial independence of the verification organization [6], and DO-178C scales required verification activities and their independence with the software level [7]. Knight and Leveson showed experimentally that independently developed program versions fail in correlated ways, so that nominal independence does not imply statistical independence of failures [33]. Assurance cases structure a claim, its argument, and its supporting evidence, for example with the Goal Structuring Notation [34, 35]. Our framework adapts these ideas to a setting they did not anticipate: a non-human producer that optimizes against its own evaluator and whose verifier may share its failure modes. Finally, Zave and Jackson distinguish requirements, specifications, and domain assumptions [36], a distinction we use to separate the gaps in Section III.

## III Why Self-Validation Fails

## III-A Setting and Notation

Let $R$ denote the stakeholder requirement, $S$ the written specification, $W$ the assumptions about the deployment environment, and $P$ the program produced by an agent. Following Zave and Jackson [36], a correct development satisfies $S\wedge W\models R$ and $P\models S$ . A test suite $T$ is a finite set of pairs $(x,o)$ where $x$ is an input or interaction sequence and $o$ is an oracle; we write $\mathit{acc}_{T}(P)$ when $P$ passes every test in $T$ . We distinguish a visible suite $T_{v}$ , available to the builder, from a hidden suite $T_{h}$ derived from the same specification and never exposed to the builder.

In self-validation, the builder forms an interpretation $\hat{S}$ of $S$ , produces $P$ and a suite $T_{b}$ from $\hat{S}$ , and iterates until $\mathit{acc}_{T_{v}\cup T_{b}}(P)$ holds. The release signal is that predicate.

## III-B Tests Become Rewards

Once $\mathit{acc}_{T_{v}}$ terminates the loop, it operates as a reward. Any program in the set $\{P\mid\mathit{acc}_{T_{v}}(P)\}$ ends the episode, and that set is far larger than $\{P\mid P\models S\}$ because $T_{v}$ samples a small part of the input space. The agent has no incentive to distinguish the two sets, and capable agents demonstrably exploit the difference [10, 11]. We define the evaluation gap of a development process over a task set as

 $\Delta_{\mathit{eval}}=\Pr\big[\mathit{acc}_{T_{v}}(P)\big]-\Pr\big[\mathit{acc}_{T_{h}}(P)\big],$

which is positive when visible success overstates correctness with respect to the same specification.

## III-C Consistency Is Not Correctness

The second failure mode does not require any optimization pressure. If $\hat{S}\neq S$ , then $P$ and $T_{b}$ can agree with each other while both disagree with $S$ . The builder’s tests then confirm the builder’s misunderstanding. This is a correlated, or common-mode, failure in the sense of Knight and Leveson [33]: two artifacts produced from the same interpretation fail on the same inputs. Separating test generation into another agent [29] reduces this correlation only if the second agent does not inherit $\hat{S}$ , for example by reading the builder’s code, rationale, or tests. Using the same underlying model may preserve part of the correlation even with separated contexts, since the two agents share training data and inductive biases. Whether context separation suffices, or whether model diversity is also needed, is an empirical question that we address in RQ2.

Incomplete self-evidence. A third failure mode occurs even when $\hat{S}=S$ . The builder can implement $S$ correctly and still test only part of it: $T_{b}$ exercises the behaviors the builder had in mind, and the others are correct without evidence. A later change that breaks them passes $T_{b}$ . Self-validation cannot reveal this gap, because the builder chooses what to test with the same attention that missed it.

## III-D Four Gaps Between Intent and Production

Table I decomposes the distance between $R$ and production behavior into four gaps. Verification against the specification can close only the conformance gap. The evaluation gap is closed by withholding the assurance artifacts from the builder. The requirement and model gaps cannot be closed by verification alone, because both concern whether $S$ and $W$ are the right objects to verify against. Our framework therefore does not claim to close them; it makes them explicit and assigns them to human approval and to runtime feedback.

## IV-A Separation of Powers

The framework assigns three roles. The builder produces $P$ . The verifier produces evidence about $P$ against $S$ . The human approves what must be demonstrated and decides whether the evidence suffices. Five principles govern the relation between roles.

P1 

No self-certification. Artifacts produced by the build plane, including the builder’s tests, never count as evidence on their own.

P2 

Information asymmetry. Assurance artifacts are withheld from the builder. The builder receives only reproducible counterexamples, which prevents the assurance suite from becoming the new reward surface.

P3 

Specification before code. Phase A evidence is derived and frozen before the verifier observes $P$ .

P4 

Verify, do not repair. The verifier demonstrates defects but does not fix them. A verifier that repairs becomes a second builder and inherits the builder’s incentives.

P5 

Explicit residual uncertainty. Evidence is reported per requirement with what was not verified, and the release decision remains human.

We adapt the three dimensions of independence in IEEE Std 1012 [6] to agents. Technical independence concerns context and model: the verifier does not share the builder’s conversation, rationale, or artifacts, and may use a different model. Managerial independence requires that the verifier is not invoked, configured, or terminated by the builder’s orchestration loop. Incentive independence, the agentic counterpart of financial independence, requires that the verifier’s objective is not tied to the builder’s success; a verifier rewarded for a green pipeline has the same incentive as the builder.

Abstract

Reviewer lottery error describes error due to a small set of peer reviews attending to only some of the issues with a paper that a larger pool of eligible reviewers would raise. We show this error can be reduced by surfacing a checklist of criticisms learned from a historical review corpus. Our approach generates a tree of checklists representing coarsenings of the atomic review claim space, then selects the coarsening that maximizes a theoretically-motivated measure of correlated agreement among reviewers. We realize this approach with an LLM-assisted pipeline and test it on NeurIPS 2021 and ICLR 2022 review data. In simulated review with LLM reviewers, the learned checklist reduces the mean squared error (MSE) of a three-reviewer committee by 58% on NeurIPS and 21% on ICLR, and on both venues the checklist with the highest correlated agreement has the lowest error for committees of three or more. In a human study with 20 participants, the learned NeurIPS checklist lowers the MSE of a paper ranking, measured against the NeurIPS 2021 order, from 0.48 to 0.22.

## 1 Introduction

Peer review systems have long played the role of a quality control mechanism for scientific production. However, human peer review is far from being a perfect system, as a result of bias, poor incentives, limited expertise, and other issues [Mann et al., 2025, Shah, 2022].
One recognized problem is reviewer lottery variance: a different assignment of qualified reviewers may have resulted in a different outcome. “Luck of the draw” effects have been demonstrated across various fields [Cole et al., 1981, Mayo et al., 2006, Beygelzimer et al., 2023, Cortes and Lawrence, 2021]. For example, the paired-committee 2021 NeurIPS reviewing experiment found that the two committees disagreed on 23% of papers, and that roughly half of the accepted papers would have been replaced if review assignments were rerun [Beygelzimer et al., 2023]. Beyond differences in expertise and in how reviewers perceive the paper, variance can arise because any single reviewer covers only a small portion of the evaluation space [Deng et al., 2026].

More severely, as LLMs increase scientific production [Kusumegi et al., 2025], higher reviewing loads per human reviewer increase noise, instigating a “review death spiral” that further incentivizes authors to try their luck by submitting weak papers [Bergstrom and Gross, 2026, Liu and Tan, 2026].

LLMs have been proposed as part of the solution [Liang et al., 2024, Xu et al., 2025, Wei et al., 2026]. For example, by systematically conducting and surfacing a broad set of checks across papers, AI reviewers can reduce lottery variance by compensating for the limited attention and idiosyncrasies of individual human reviewers. This ensures a common set of baseline checks is applied to each paper, while still allowing the individual reviewers to exercise their judgment and expertise in weighing surfaced issues and identifying other aspects of the paper to assess. However, the risk that must be balanced is that a shared representation evaluating the paper can introduce bias by causing reviewers to underweight their private information [Bikhchandani et al., 1992, Stasser and Titus, 1985, see, e.g.,].

We first characterize the problem of designing an AI checklist as identifying a representation of the review claim space that, when applied to a paper, reproducibly reduces lottery variance without increasing overall error via the addition of shared bias. We formalize checklist design as learning a coarsened representation of the review claim space observed in historical reviews. Because historical peer review datasets do not enable estimating reviewer decisions under checklists that reviewers didn’t observe, our approach targets the coarsening that maximizes a proxy objective based in correlated agreement: agreement between independent reviews of the same paper relative to the expected agreement between reviews of different papers.

We next contribute an automated pipeline for learning and implementing checklists using LLM agents. Our approach takes as input a historical review corpus, and decomposes each review into atomic claims, each labeled by the source of information that would resolve it. We require the claims to be settled by the paper or its supplementary material, such that an LLM can verify the learned checklist with high accuracy. The claims are then grouped across papers into a hierarchy of named checklist items, and our proxy objective selects the granularity at which that hierarchy is applied.

We evaluate whether checklists learned using our correlated agreement objective reduce finite-reviewer error on existing review datasets. In a simulated review experiment with LLMs on 30 papers each from NeurIPS 2021 and ICLR 2022, we find that for a typical committee of three reviewers, the learned checklist reduces the review error by 58% on NeurIPS and 21% on ICLR. On NeurIPS 2021, it also has lower error than the official NeurIPS 2021 paper checklist at every committee size. On both datasets, the checklist with the highest correlated agreement also has the lowest error for committees of three or more reviewers, so our proxy objective identifies the checklist that best balances variance reduction and bias addition.

## 2 Related Work

Human peer review has played the role of an imperfect quality control mechanism for scientific production for over a century [Mann et al., 2025, Shah, 2022]. Reviewer lottery effects are demonstrated in grant funding by replicating review processes and finding that outcomes depend on the draw [Cole et al., 1981, Mayo et al., 2006]. In machine learning, a reanalysis of the 2014 duplicated assignment NeurIPS experiment attributes half of the variation in reviewer quality scores to reviewer subjectivity [Cortes and Lawrence, 2021]. The 2021 NeurIPS experiment finds substantial variation in accepted papers across two non-communicating committees who reviewed the same 882 papers [Beygelzimer et al., 2023]. Computational interventions proposed to address lottery issues have tended to target assignment, calibration, and dishonest behavior rather than what reviewers attend to [Shah, 2022].

AI reviewers bring opportunities and risks. LLM-generated comments can overlap human reviews at rates comparable to a second human reviewer [Liang et al., 2024], and models can perform well on targeted, verifiable questions [Liu and Shah, 2023]. State-of-the-art AI review systems increasingly rely on agentic, multi-stage pipelines that ground their comments in quoted passages or other verifiable evidence to improve interpretability and accuracy [Gao et al., 2025, Nguyen et al., 2026, Weng et al., 2026, Fang et al., 2026, Ma et al., 2026, Chicago Human+AI Lab, 2026, Reviewer3, 2026, Jiang and Ng, 2025]. Given the infeasibility of large scale human peer review studies, such tools are often tested via recall of implanted defects; others propose LLM simulations as a testbed for peer review mechanisms that can recover aggregate dynamics of human peer review feedback and outcomes [Jin et al., 2024].
Venues have also begun to experiment with AI in review, including LLM feedback on reviewers’ written reviews [Thakkar et al., 2025], LLM reviews returned to authors [Biswas and Sahu, 2026], and LLM review assistants in OpenReview [Biswas and Charlin, 2026].

However, AI reviewers can be gameable [Baumann et al., 2026], can hallucinate [Deng et al., 2026], and attend unevenly across review dimensions, over-weighting technical validity and under-weighting novelty [Shin et al., 2025]. Applying consistent summary representations also contributes bias, by attempting to reduce scientific quality to a finite set of proxies that can cause reviewers to undervalue their private knowledge [Bikhchandani et al., 1992, Stasser and Titus, 1985].

## 3 Problem: Learning a Checklist to Reduce Lottery Variance

We present a model of peer review and the problem of reviewer lottery variance. We formulate the task of learning a checklist to reduce variance from a historical peer review corpus.

## 3.1 Reviewer Lottery Variance

One way to frame the goal of peer review is to uncover the latent true epistemic quality of a paper. However, even if a ground truth paper quality state could be said to exist, it would be unobservable.

Thus, a more realistic formalization of the goal of peer review is to recover the expected assessment of the paper taken over the eligible reviewer population. The problem is that we can typically only observe the assessments of a small subset of the ideal group of reviewers.

We define the population review target for a given paper $i$ as the mean assessment under the distribution of eligible reviewers for that paper:

 $\mu_{i}=\mathbb{E}_{r\sim P_{i}}[Y_{ir}],$ 

where $r\sim P_{i}$ represents a random reviewer draw from the population of eligible reviewers for paper $i$ and $Y_{ir}$ is the judgment of an unaided reviewer $r$ on paper $i$ . While in practice $Y_{ir}$ could take various forms, including multi-dimensional assessments like rubric-style evaluations, for the purposes of formalizing the problem we assume that $Y_{ir}\in\mathbb{R}$ is a scalar representing a final paper score. A peer review system that targets $m$ reviewers per paper estimates $\mu_{i}$ as:

 $\mathbf{R}_{im}=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{m})\sim P_{i}^{(m)};\qquad\bar{Y}_{im}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}Y_{ir_{j}};$ 

where $P_{i}^{(m)}$ is the reviewer assignment mechanism. While $\mathbb{E}[\bar{Y}_{im}]=\mu_{i}$ , any downstream decisions that rely on aggregated reviewer assessments are subject to sampling error, where the small values of $m$ that are typical in human peer review can yield estimates far from $\mu_{i}$ .

Lottery variance may arise as a result of each reviewer’s expertise being specialized relative to the range of expertise across eligible reviewers, or reviewers having limited time or cognitive resources to spend surfacing issues, or from some reviewers making errors in interpreting aspects of the paper.

## Estimating Reviewer Variance and Incorrect Criticism on the NeurIPS 2021 Experiment

To motivate our characterization of errors in human peer review, we contribute a novel claim-level analysis of the NeurIPS 2021 dual-committee experiment. We use the overlap between issues across the two independent committees for each paper, after merging common issues, to estimate impacts of lottery variance at the claim level. Full details are in Appendix B.

We found that independent reviewers rarely mention the same issue, and that many concrete criticisms (those that can be checked directly against the paper) are refuted by the paper materials. Specifically:

• 

Low coverage: One reviewer raises about 6% of the distinct issues that further reviewers drawn from the same pool would eventually raise (6.4%, 95% CI $[5.9,6.9]$ , Chao2 richness [Chao, 1987]).

• 

Low overlap: Only one third of reviewer claims are also raised by the other committee (34.3%, 95% CI $[32.8,35.8]$ ), and 81% of issues are raised by a single reviewer (Appendix B).

• 

False criticisms: The paper itself clearly refutes 18.2% of all judged concrete claims (95% CI $[16.3,20.2]$ ).11

These results suggest that one reviewer raises only a small share of the issues this reviewer pool would eventually surface, and that humans make mistakes in a non-trivial proportion of review claims.

We seek to reduce reviewer lottery variance by introducing a shared checklist $g$ .
A checklist consists of a set of binary claims that can be resolved against the paper materials with high accuracy and surfaced for assigned reviewers. In doing so, it stands to reduce variance arising from sources like reviewer myopia or careless mistakes.
Introducing a checklist as intervention results in $Y_{ir}(g)$ at the individual reviewer level, with checklist-assisted population mean $\mu_{i}(g)=\mathbb{E}_{r\sim P_{i}}[Y_{ir}(g)]$ (where the no checklist target can similarly be written as $\mu_{i}(\varnothing)=\mathbb{E}_{r\sim P_{i}}[Y_{ir}(\varnothing)]$ ).

That is, the total error induced by the checklist will be less than that observed under no checklist. Intuitively, a checklist can reduce variance insofar as variation across reviewer scores results from variation in which issues reviewers notice or the possibility of careless mistakes checking a verifiable issue against the paper.
However, by exposing all reviewers to a shared representation, introducing a checklist may also systematically shift their assessments away from the unaided population review target by biasing what information reviewers pay attention to or how they weight it.

## 3.3 Checklist Selection

Existing review corpora provide a rich source for learning what kinds of concerns human reviewers perceive as important.
But how should we identify the set of relevant checkable issues from which a checklist can draw? Simply distilling the space of atomic review claims from peer review corpora into checklist items would face multiple problems. First, issues learned directly from human reviews may be value judgments rather than properties verifiable against the paper or supplement, which is where LLM checks are most reliable. We therefore want to restrict to those issues that can be directly resolved by the paper materials. Second, if atomic review claims are framed too specifically or idiosyncratically, they may not capture reproducible signal in human review, and add bias if instituted across reviewers. Such a checklist could also be prohibitively large for human reviewers to process, so that only those that apply to a given paper are surfaced.

title: Beyond source attribution: Address authorship and comparability decisions in an LLM-built scholarly knowledge graph
abstract: A knowledge graph needs a stable address for its evidence even where the literature offers competing classifications and agrees on none. Yet an address chosen for retrieval readily passes for the only classification available. This happens whenever records gathered under one name concern units that differ in boundaries, rank, or the criteria by which they are described or counted. In Sinitic dialectology the same localities recur in schemes whose units differ in membership and rank, and a unit may change its affiliation when the evidence for its diagnosis changes. Two tone counts, each quoted faithfully, may still count different things. The taxonomy of an entire field thus comes to rest on the unstable frame of a literature that contradicts itself. Neither verifying a quotation nor searching for conflicting values detects these differences. I distinguish the working address that gathers candidate evidence, the category that the source defines and the decision that admits a passage to a particular comparison, and argue that such decisions, together with the dependence among records, belong to the provenance of a comparison. On four re-runnable cases, the accompanying PaRAGraph Casebook shows where such differences arise among claims extracted by a language model and verified before entering the graph. The platform now stores the corresponding decisions as objects for one dimension of comparability, the address of a record: the placement of a locality in each source's scheme, the decision that a name in a given publication denotes a unit rather than a place, and the origin of every address. The working taxonomy can then be revised as new sources yield new claims, while the path from each comparison to its evidence stays fixed. Keywords: knowledge graphs; source attribution; classification; claim extraction; comparative concepts; Sinitic dialectology; Yue
