Abstract

How much can we trust an agent to find the paper we need? As researchers, we search the literature from what we have read toward what we have not. We thus describe what we want in our own terms, which a paper may show only implicitly; our requirements grow as we read; and what we seek may lie in an empty region no paper yet covers. We introduce CompLit, a literature search benchmark spanning all eight arXiv domains, with one diagnostic setting for each of these needs. The strongest agents, Codex (GPT-5.6-Sol) and Claude Code (Opus 4.8), answer 86–87% of Standard queries, yet fall to 66–68% when requirements are implicit (Implicit), lose another 6 and 15pp, respectively, as they accumulate (Cumulative), and abstain on at most 53% of the queries no paper satisfies (Unmet). No agent leads in every domain, and all are less accurate on papers from before 2019 or after 2023. Tracing their search, we find that agents often reach the right paper, or the closest one, yet misjudge it. Doing well on CompLit is a step toward agents that we can trust to find the paper we need, or to tell us that none exists.

## 1 Introduction

Researchers increasingly ask agents such as OpenAI Deep Research, Codex, or Claude Code to find papers they need (OpenAI, 2025; Anthropic, 2025). The paper an agent returns shapes what they build on, what they cite, and whether they consider their ideas new
(Greenberg, 2009; Pavlovic et al., 2021).

Despite these stakes, most literature search benchmarks (Table 1) evaluate agents from the paper’s side rather than the researcher’s. They build each query from a target paper, so it reuses the paper’s terms, the whole request comes in a single query, and a matching paper always exists. Such queries are thus bound to the target paper: its wording, a single request, and an existing answer.

Figure 1: 
Frontier agents on CompLit. All four agents score well on Standard (mean 81.4%) but drop on every diagnostic setting (arrows: drop in mean). On Unmet, accuracy is the rate of correct abstention.

Figure 2: Motivation and overview of CompLit. Top: as a researcher reads retrieved papers, their need proves implicit, cumulative, and unmet: the required property is rarely stated outright, each new requirement rules out earlier candidates, and the full set may match no paper. Bottom: our three diagnostic settings test whether (i) an agent infers such a property from paper evidence, (ii) reassesses earlier answers as requirements accumulate, and (iii) abstains when no paper meets the need.

Researchers, however, search outward, from what they have explored toward what they have not (Kuhlthau, 1991). Because they frame requirements from where they stand, the paper they seek may state them only implicitly (Dasigi et al., 2021); as they read on, requirements accumulate (Vakkari, 2001); and as they seek what no one has explored, their need may be unmet (Asai and Choi, 2021).

In Figure 2, a medical imaging researcher cannot send patient scans outside the hospital. After reading how DeepSeek-R1-Zero learns to reason through reinforcement learning alone (Guo et al., 2025), they look for a method that does the same in-house. A matching paper often describes how it trains without explicitly stating that it does so in-house (implicit). Reading that such a paper tests only on X-ray, the researcher also asks for CT and MRI, ruling it out (cumulative). If no paper meets them all, the direction may still be open (unmet).

We introduce CompLit, a benchmark for compositional scientific literature search that evaluates agents in these situations. Alongside a Standard reference setting close to existing benchmarks, it has one diagnostic setting per need, each requiring a distinct ability. Implicit requires an agent to infer whether a paper meets a requirement from how the paper describes its work. Cumulative requires an agent to reassess its earlier answers and move beyond them as requirements accumulate over turns. Unmet requires an agent to abstain when no paper satisfies every requirement.

We compose each query from several requirements taken from survey comparison tables, and collect 870 single-turn queries and 220 conversations, all manually verified, across all eight arXiv domains. Beyond final accuracy and its breakdown by domain and publication year, CompLit traces agents’ search dynamics over tool calls or turns for each setting, pinpointing where they go wrong.

The strongest agents already reach 86–87% accuracy on Standard (Figure 1), where, as in existing benchmarks, most requirements are stated outright, all arrive at once, and a match always exists.
Even there, average accuracy ranges from 74% in physics to 94% in finance and economics, and falls from 88% on papers from 2019–23 to 75% on older and 80% on more recent ones (Table 3).
Beyond these gaps, each diagnostic setting reveals a different way they fall short.

On Implicit, agents struggle to infer whether a paper meets a requirement from indirect evidence. The gold paper is retrieved less often, and even when it is, agents often leave it unread, or read it and still choose another paper (Figure 3). In turn, accuracy drops 19 to 37pp, and even the best agent returns a wrong paper for about a third of queries.

On Cumulative, agents struggle to reassess their way to the right paper, with Claude Code (Opus 4.8) and Codex CLI (GPT-5.6-Sol) failing in different ways. Claude Code often leaves a wrong answer but keeps picking new wrong papers, still losing 15pp from the corresponding single-turn queries, while Codex picks a wrong paper far less often in the first place, yet still loses 6. As a result, the two, which score alike on single queries, end 11pp apart (Figure 4).

On Unmet, agents struggle to abstain when no paper qualifies. They open the paper closest to the request within ten tool calls in over 90% of queries, yet still present a paper as a match in 47% to 82% of queries (Figure 5). A researcher may thus mistake an open direction for one already taken.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

• 

We introduce CompLit to evaluate scientific literature search on researchers’ implicit, cumulative, and unmet needs across eight domains.

• 

We test thirteen baselines, from corpus retrievers to agents, reporting trends by domain and publication year.

• 

We also analyze search dynamics to pinpoint where each agent fails, not only in retrieving a paper but also in verifying it.

Literature Search Benchmarks.

Early benchmarks established natural-language retrieval as a setting for scientific literature search. LitSearch (Ajith et al., 2024) and PaSa (He et al., 2025) generate queries automatically from citation contexts, each adding a smaller researcher-written set, and PaperFindingBench and LitQA2-Search (Bragg et al., 2026) draw queries from real user logs and from biology questions. Each of these benchmarks poses a request as a single need rather than a composition of constraints.

Multi-Constraint Queries.

A complementary line structures complex needs into multiple aspects or conditions. DORIS-MAE (Wang et al., 2023) decomposes scientific queries into hierarchical aspects, and PaSaMaster-Bench (Du et al., 2026) pairs each expert-written intent with a checklist of criteria across six domains. Beyond scholarly search, BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025) combines hard-to-find factual web clues, while MultiConIR (Lu et al., 2025) scales queries from one to ten conditions. Recent deep-research benchmarks have brought this structure to the scientific literature. SAGE (Hu et al., 2026) composes queries from paper artifacts and citation overlaps, while AutoResearchBench (Xiong et al., 2026) derives Deep and Wide queries from target papers.

By contrast, we start from the researcher’s side, where a request requires an agent to infer evidence a paper leaves implicit, to reassess candidates as the requirements accumulate, and to abstain when no paper meets the need.

Implicit, Cumulative, and Unmet.

Each of our diagnostic settings has a counterpart outside scholarly search. Retrieval and reading comprehension benchmarks make relevance depend on facts a document states only implicitly (Taghavi et al., 2025; Tchuindjo et al., 2026). Conversational benchmarks reveal the need over turns and show that models anchor on early assumptions (Ali et al., 2026; Laban et al., 2026). Unanswerable questions test whether models abstain (Rajpurkar et al., 2018; Kirichenko et al., 2026). Scholarly search demands all three as a researcher explores what they have not: properties are rarely stated outright, requirements grow with each paper read, and their conjunction may match no paper. Yet no scholarly benchmark in Table 1 tests them. While Xiong et al. (2026) covers abstention, only 60 of its queries do so, all in computer science. CompLit tests each ability in a dedicated setting, and its analysis of search dynamics shows not only whether an agent fails but where in the search it does (§4.4).

## 3 The CompLit Benchmark

We propose CompLit, a benchmark for compositional scientific literature search. We define the task (§3.1), derive the constraints of each query (§3.2), build a Standard and three diagnostic settings (§3.3), and provide a corpus (§3.4).

## 3.1 Task Definition

A query $q$ expresses a research intent and a set of constraints $\mathcal{C}=\{c_{1},\dots,c_{k}\}$ that a paper the researcher has not yet found must satisfy jointly. A system searches a corpus $\mathcal{D}$ of papers through a fixed index or the open web.

A paper $p\in\mathcal{D}$ satisfies $c_{i}$ , written $p\models c_{i}$ , if its full paper, with figures, bibliographic record, or comparison with another paper supports $c_{i}$ , and $p\models\mathcal{C}$ if it satisfies every constraint. The gold answer is the target paper $p^{*}$ with $p^{*}\models\mathcal{C}$ , or $\varnothing$ if no paper in $\mathcal{D}$ satisfies $\mathcal{C}$ . A system returns a single paper or abstains; an answer is correct if it is $p^{*}$ , or an abstention when the gold is $\varnothing$ , and we report accuracy on each set.

## 3.2 Query Generation Pipeline

We use Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (Qwen Team, 2026) as the LLM and the VLM in every step of constraint derivation and query generation, with prompts in Appendix C.1.

Constraint sources.

We start with survey comparison tables that record each surveyed paper’s attributes. The survey authors consider distinguishing in their field, so their rows share a scope yet differ on those attributes.
Each constraint $c_{i}$ is a proposition about the target paper with a source $s_{i}\in\{\text{content},\text{figural},\text{metadata},$ $\text{comparative}\}$ .

From the table, content constraints are the cell values of the paper’s row, restated as propositions, and comparative constraints contrast the paper with another paper in the same table (e.g., broader imaging modalities).
From the paper itself, figural constraints are claims a vision-language model (VLM) reads from its figures, either quantitative (an ordering, a peak value) or qualitative (an architecture pattern, a trend), and metadata constraints are the year, categories, and authors in its arXiv record.

These sources test full-paper understanding, figure interpretation, and cross-paper comparison.

Constraint verification.

To ensure factuality and high quality, we verify every constraint exhaustively against the target paper.
When $s_{i}\in\{\text{content},\text{comparative}\}$ we do not know which part of the paper supports the constraint, so a grounder LLM reads the paper and records the supporting passage, and a verifier scores whether that passage appears in the paper and supports the constraint. When $s_{i}\in\{\text{figural},\text{metadata}\}$ , the evidence is already known: a VLM verifier scores each figural claim against its figure and caption, and metadata constraints are checked against the arXiv record.

If the verifier scores a constraint below an empirical threshold of 0.9, we reground or regenerate it and score it again for up to 10 rounds; any constraint that never passes is discarded. Every constraint that passes is then rechecked by the authors, so each clears both automatic and manual reviews.

Evidence levels.

We label every content, figural, and comparative constraint with an evidence level $\ell_{i}\in\{\text{explicit},\text{paraphrased},$ $\text{inferred}\}$ , which records how a system must ground it in the paper. We judge it against the paper for a content constraint, and against the figure for a figural one.

A constraint is explicit when the system can read the fact as it stands, and paraphrased when the system must match meaning in different words, or when the claim re-describes what the figure directly depicts. It is inferred when the system must derive the fact, because the text only implies it (e.g., training in-house), or because it follows only from comparing several visual elements (e.g., a ranking or a trend).

The inferred level also covers every comparative constraint, since establishing one requires reading a second paper. These labels are the basis of the Implicit setting (§3.3).

Query writing.

We select constraints to fit a research intent, so that a query carries only the properties a researcher would need. An intent is generated from one of 16 search purposes (Haddad et al., 2026), such as methodological guidance or comparative analysis. For each paper, we select up to three intents it can serve and verify each with the same LLM. The LLM then chooses the constraints that serve each intent and writes a request around it. We repeat generation and verification to ensure quality, and record the constraints it uses as $\mathcal{C}$ .

Human verification.

The authors then check every query three ways: each constraint’s recorded evidence must be in the paper and support the constraint; the assigned intent must fit the paper and claim nothing the paper does not support; and the query must identify the target.

Uniqueness check.

We then check automatically that every gold paper is the only known match. For each query, we retrieve the top-50 papers with both BM25 (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009) and Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Zhang et al., 2025), and the LLM judges whether any of the 100 papers satisfies all constraints. We remove a query if any paper other than the target does, or if any paper at all does for an Unmet query. This removed 5.5%, 4.3%, and 1.0% of queries in Standard, Implicit, and Unmet, respectively.

## 3.3 Diagnostic Settings

The settings follow how a literature search unfolds. Alongside Standard, each setting evaluates one challenge.

Standard.

This setting, close to existing benchmarks, serves as a reference for the diagnostic settings. Queries state constraints at all evidence levels, given at once, and every query has a target. This set supports analysis across domains, publication years, and numbers of constraints. It contains 350 queries over 251 target papers.

Implicit.

This setting tests whether a system can infer that a paper meets requirements it states only implicitly. Every constraint must be inferred: $\ell_{i}=\text{inferred}$ for every $c_{i}\in\mathcal{C}$ , so queries carry no metadata constraints. No constraint can then be resolved by lexical or semantic matching. Rather, each must be reasoned out from what the paper reports or from how it compares to a named paper. It contains 220 queries over 179 papers.

Cumulative.

This setting tests whether a system reassesses its earlier answers as requirements accumulate over turns. The need is revealed over multiple turns: following Laban et al. (2026), we rebuild each Implicit query into a conversation of 3 to 5 turns. An offline scheduler (gpt-5.6-sol (OpenAI, 2026a)) partitions $\mathcal{C}$ into disjoint subsets $\mathcal{C}^{(1)},\dots,\mathcal{C}^{(T)}$ , one per turn with one to three constraints each, and writes the user utterance for each turn in advance.

At evaluation time, a gpt-5.4-mini (OpenAI, 2026b) user simulator at temperature 0 delivers each utterance, so every system faces the same conversation with the same constraints at each turn Laban et al. (2026). The system may answer at every turn and is scored on its final answer, once all of $\mathcal{C}$ has been revealed, with per-turn answers kept for analysis. This set contains 220 conversations.

Unmet.

This setting tests whether a system abstains when no paper meets every requirement.
We construct queries as in Standard and retain those answered correctly by all three reference systems, chosen for their low cost: Harness-1 (Jiang et al., 2026), DeepSeek-V4-Pro (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), and GLM-5.2 (GLM-5-Team, 2026).

Constraints and queries are generated and verified automatically, but we check every constraint and every query by hand to remove remaining errors. Finally, open-web agents search a live web, so their results may shift slightly if the experiments are rerun.
conclusion:
We introduced CompLit, a benchmark that evaluates agents in the way researchers search: outward from what they have read, with needs that are implicit, cumulative, or unmet. Even the strongest agents lose about 20 points when every constraint is implicit and fall further, each in a different way, as requirements accumulate, while most agents accept a near-miss instead of abstaining. Beyond final accuracy, CompLit traces each agent’s search step by step, revealing where these failures arise: agents often reach the right paper, or the closest one, yet misjudge it. An agent that does well here can be trusted to find the paper that meets a need, or to say that none does.

Looking ahead, we envision two directions. One is a harness for literature search, guided by where each agent fails and which papers it finds hard. The other is a world model of a field, distilled from surveys, so that an agent knows how to search a field and check a condition before the search begins. We hope CompLit serves as a foundation for future work on scientific literature search.

Abstract

Future-work statements offer a record of the questions researchers choose to leave open. Using them to describe a field, however, requires separating thematic change from changes in document coverage, topic assignment, and scholarly writing. FutureLens examines these measurement issues in a recovered snapshot of 5,655 ACL papers published during 2012–2022, including 4,005 with supplied future-work reference text. We compare non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) and latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA), aggregate topic presence at the paper level, and examine normalized prevalence, exploratory trend statistics, assignment stability, and agreement between input-derived text and references. Across available seeds, NMF has higher mean normalized pointwise mutual information (0.1387 versus 0.1280) and higher pairwise assignment stability, while LDA has greater keyword diversity (0.8900 versus 0.7750). Seed-zero results show increasing prevalence of broad model-training and question-related vocabulary, alongside substantial citation and document-structure content. Mean input/reference topic-set overlap is 0.5191 for NMF and 0.4924 for LDA; temporal rank agreement varies widely and does not imply agreement in prevalence levels. These findings support a descriptive account of the available corpus, with explicit qualifications for missing references, incomplete runs, and unverified reference provenance. The contribution is an empirical measurement study of longitudinal scholarly signals, not a new topic-modeling algorithm or a forecasting system.

## 1 Introduction

Scientific papers document both completed work and unfinished questions.
Their future-work statements occupy a distinctive rhetorical position:
authors identify unresolved problems, possible extensions, or resources
they would like to develop. Previous studies have analyzed these statements
to characterize proposed research directions and differences across NLP
tasks Qian et al. (2021); Zhang et al. (2023). Aggregating these statements can help
readers inspect how a research community describes its open agenda.
This complements analyses of publication text and citation
patterns Anderson et al. (2012), but it does not establish which proposed
directions are subsequently pursued.

The distinction matters for Science of Science. A rise in mentions can
reflect more publications, better recovery of future-work text, a change
in terminology, or a change in the underlying research agenda. Topic
interpretation also requires care: statistical model performance does
not necessarily correspond to human judgments of
interpretability Chang et al. (2009). Automatic coherence measures provide
useful evidence about topic quality Lau et al. (2014), but a cluster with
a plausible title may still contain routine experimental language rather
than a coherent scientific problem. Even when two text sources exhibit
similar temporal rankings, they may differ substantially in how often
they mention the corresponding topic. A useful longitudinal analysis
must expose these alternatives before interpreting its output as
evidence about scientific priorities.

FutureLens investigates how reliably future-work statements
can characterize the evolution of research themes within a
scientific community. We examine 5,655 ACL papers published
between 2012 and 2022, including 4,005 papers with available
future-work references. Using non-negative matrix factorization
(NMF) Lee and Seung (1999) and latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) Blei et al. (2003), we analyze the
reliability of topic representations, identify longitudinal
patterns in expressed future directions, and examine their
relationship with the themes of current scholarly research.
Rather than treating changes in topic prevalence as direct
evidence of shifting scientific priorities, we investigate
how corpus coverage, topic-model variability, and textual
artifacts constrain their interpretation. Our analysis is
descriptive and does not establish whether proposed research
directions are subsequently pursued.

Our study addresses three research questions.
RQ1: How reliably can topic models identify and characterize
research themes in scholarly publications and future-work statements?
We examine differences between NMF and LDA in topic coherence,
keyword diversity, and assignment stability across random seeds.
RQ2: How have research themes expressed in ACL future-work
statements evolved from 2012 to 2022, and how do corpus coverage
and topic content affect their interpretation?
We analyze normalized topic prevalence and longitudinal trends
while accounting for incomplete reference coverage and potential
textual artifacts.
RQ3: To what extent do future-work statements reflect
the themes of current scholarly research?
We investigate topic overlap at the paper level and temporal
agreement between scholarly input text and future-work references,
distinguishing similarities in trend direction from differences
in topic prevalence.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we provide a comparative
evaluation of NMF and LDA for characterizing scholarly research
themes, distinguishing topic coherence, keyword diversity, and
assignment stability from semantic validity. Second, we present
a coverage-aware longitudinal analysis of future-work statements
in ACL publications from 2012 to 2022, identifying prominent
thematic patterns while examining the effects of reference
availability, topic content, and temporal variation. Third, we
analyze the relationship between current scholarly research
and expressed future directions through paper-level topic overlap
and temporal source agreement. Together, these contributions
provide an empirical framework for interpreting longitudinal
scholarly signals while recognizing the limitations of incomplete
coverage, model sensitivity, and unverified reference provenance.

## 2 Related work and positioning

Longitudinal topic analysis of scientific literature.
Computational histories of NLP already use publication text to study changes in research activity. Anderson et al. Anderson et al. (2012) analyze the ACL’s intellectual history, while Pramanick et al. Pramanick et al. (2023) study paradigm shifts through a framework involving causal discovery and inference. Our narrower focus is the measurement relationship between input-derived scholarly text and supplied future-work references; our recovered results do not support causal inference.

Future-work statements.
Qian et al. Qian et al. (2021) use future-work sentences to explore
research trends across NLP tasks. Zhang et al. Zhang et al. (2023)
develop recognition and classification methods, examine
future-work content, and compare it with abstracts of
subsequent research. Yang et al. Yang et al. (2025) identify
emerging topics through entity novelty in future-work
sentences. FutureGen Al Azher et al. (2025) employs an
LLM-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approach
to generate future-work suggestions from scholarly texts.
Future-work analysis and its connection to research
evolution are therefore established research directions.
FutureLens examines a complementary measurement question:
how model sensitivity, reference coverage, and source
disagreement affect longitudinal interpretation.
We distinguish same-year trajectory agreement from
subsequent uptake and make no claim to identify emerging
entities or predict their adoption.

Topic models and interpretation.
LDA models documents through latent topic mixtures Blei et al. (2003); NMF decomposes nonnegative representations into additive components Lee and Seung (1999). Dynamic topic models explicitly allow topic representations to change with time Blei and Lafferty (2006). Here, a fixed representation within each descriptive fit makes annual prevalence comparable, at the cost of imposing a retrospective vocabulary. Neither this design nor the use of topic labels constitutes a new modeling algorithm.

LLM-assisted interpretation also has direct precedents. LimTopic combines topic modeling and language-model-based interpretation for limitations in scientific articles Al Azher et al. (2024). We treat generated titles as reading aids attached to recovered keyword lists. They do not change topic assignments and are not independent evidence that a topic is meaningful. This separation is consistent with the broader distinction between model fit and human interpretability Chang et al. (2009). Automatic coherence measures can assist evaluation Lau et al. (2014), but our study does not substitute them for an annotation experiment.

Prior studies examine future-work identification,
emerging topics, and longitudinal scholarly trends.
FutureLens complements these approaches by jointly
examining topic-model reliability, corpus coverage,
and agreement between current research and supplied
future-work references. This measurement-oriented
analysis clarifies how these factors constrain
the interpretation of longitudinal scholarly signals.

patterns within a relatively coherent scientific community,
where changes in research tasks, methodologies, and terminology
can be studied within a shared disciplinary context.
The 2012–2022 observation period reflects the available
recovered experimental snapshot rather than the complete
historical or contemporary coverage of ACL publications.

## 3.2 Text sources and recovered runs

We distinguish input-derived activity text from supplied reference text. The former is a textual proxy for the research discussed in a paper, not an external observation of scientific activity. The inspected pipeline constructs ACL input from the abstract and six supplied text fields. Its activity transformation removes exact reference sentences and selected future-work cues. References come from the supplied Future_Work field; the report labels their source acl_supplied and records no fallback. This processing does not establish whether references were manually extracted, automatically extracted, or edited upstream. We therefore avoid the term “ground truth.” The report contains three run variants associated with Gemma, Mistral, and Qwen topic labeling. All lack completion markers. NMF has five available seeds in each; LDA has four in the Gemma and Mistral variants and three in the Qwen variant. Matching numerical outputs are not three independent experiments: these language models only title topics in this pipeline. We use the first listed, Gemma-labeled snapshot as the reporting reference, without pooling variants. Its five NMF and four LDA seeds determine the method summaries. Detailed descriptive tables use seed zero, the lowest seed with such outputs, rather than the highest-scoring seed.
No usable BERTopic outputs, forecasting records, silhouette values, or human judgments are recovered. Missing values remain unavailable. We do not import numerical results from the earlier, differently configured 2012–2024 manuscript into this 2012–2022 comparison. Appendix A explains the evidence and implementation boundary.

## 4 Preliminary BERTopic Exploration

An earlier FutureLens analysis applied BERTopic
independently to yearly ACL future-work collections
from 2012–2024, identifying themes such as machine
translation, multilingual processing, and evaluation.
However, independently fitted yearly clusters lack
consistent topic identities, and raw frequencies
are sensitive to corpus size. These limitations
motivate our present analysis using a shared topic
space within each fit and normalized prevalence.
The preliminary results are not combined with
the current NMF/LDA comparison.

## 5 Problem formulation and analysis design

## 5.1 Common topic space and paper-level presence

Let $D_{t}$ denote analyzed papers in year $t$ , with $N_{t}=|D_{t}|$ . For paper $i$ , let $A_{i}$ denote activity text, $R_{i}$ supplied reference text, and $m_{i}$ indicate whether $R_{i}$ is available. Each model and seed defines its own topic set $\mathcal{K}=\{0,\ldots,19\}$ . The inspected implementation fits the descriptive topic space on deduplicated sentence units pooled from activity and reference text across years. The recovered stability tables compare 1,168,951 identical training units. These units are not additional papers or independent temporal observations.

For NMF, the implementation uses TF–IDF features, random initialization, and up to 400 iterations.
LDA uses count features, batch learning, and up to 20 iterations. Both models use English stop-word
removal and a maximum vocabulary of 20,000 features.

We fix $K=20$ for both models to ensure comparable
thematic granularity. This is a controlled
experimental choice, not an empirically optimized
topic count. As different topic counts may alter
thematic structures and longitudinal patterns,
our findings remain conditional on this specification.
The comparison also varies feature representations
and modeling algorithms.

Each sentence receives its maximum-weight topic; zero-feature units receive label $-1$ . A paper’s topic set $T_{i}^{S}$ , for source $S\in\{A,R\}$ , is the union of nonnegative sentence labels. Define $z_{ikt}^{S}=\mathbb{1}[k\in T_{i}^{S}]$ . A topic is counted at most once per paper, although a paper can contain many topics. Consequently, topic prevalences need not sum to one. Longer text offers more opportunities to acquire topics even under this binary aggregation.

The global descriptive fit keeps topic identifiers fixed across years within a model and seed. It does not align identifiers across NMF and LDA or across seeds. Because later text contributes to the fit, a topic containing a later term such as BERT may also absorb earlier, more generic model-training sentences. Its 2012 prevalence cannot be interpreted as evidence that the later technology was present then.

## 5.2 Two denominators answer different questions

The recovered trend tables use all analyzed papers:

 $P_{kt}^{A}=\frac{\sum_{i\in D_{t}}z_{ikt}^{A}}{N_{t}},\qquad P_{kt}^{R,\mathrm{all}}=\frac{\sum_{i\in D_{t}:m_{i}=1}z_{ikt}^{R}}{N_{t}}.$ 

(1)

The second quantity measures observed reference-topic coverage among all analyzed papers. Missing references contribute no observed topic occurrence, but are not verified topic absences. Let $M_{t}=\sum_{i\in D_{t}}m_{i}$ , $c_{t}=M_{t}/N_{t}$ , and $P_{kt}^{R,\mathrm{obs}}$ be prevalence among papers with references. Then

 $P_{kt}^{R,\mathrm{all}}=c_{t}P_{kt}^{R,\mathrm{obs}}.$ 

(2)

This identity separates reference availability from topic prevalence conditional on availability. Normalization removes the direct effect of corpus size; it does not remove missingness bias. We retain the reported all-paper series when presenting its saved statistics and use available-reference endpoint calculations only as explicitly identified denominator checks.

For temporal source agreement, the pipeline instead restricts both sources to the same papers, $D_{t}^{*}=\{i\in D_{t}:m_{i}=1\}$ . We denote these paired prevalences by $\widetilde{P}_{kt}^{A}$ and $\widetilde{P}_{kt}^{R}$ , each with denominator $M_{t}$ . These are different estimands from the all-paper activity series and reference coverage in Equation 1.

## 5.3 Quality, stability, and trends

Recovered coherence uses binary word co-occurrence over saved training text units. For two topic keywords $u,v$ , normalized pointwise mutual information is

 $\operatorname{NPMI}(u,v)=\frac{\log[p(u,v)/(p(u)p(v))]}{-\log p(u,v)}.$ 

(3)

The report reconstructs NPMI from saved text and diversity from saved keywords. Diversity is the fraction of distinct words across the top-ten keyword lists for all 20 topics. Both are intrinsic summaries, not measures of factual accuracy or historical validity. Across seeds, we report means and sample standard deviations using only available observations.

Assignment stability is adjusted Rand index (ARI) Hubert and Arabie (1985) between seed pairs on identical training units, including the outlier label. ARI compares partitions without requiring matching topic identifiers. The pairs share seeds and are dependent; we summarize their range without treating them as independent replications. Assignment stability also does not establish stability of a particular named topic’s trajectory.

The Sen slope summarizes pairwise annual prevalence changes Sen (1968):

(4)

limitations:
FutureLens reveals increasing prevalence of broad
model-training and question-related themes, alongside
declining syntax-related content and substantial
textual artifacts. These findings highlight three
distinct measurement considerations: intrinsic
topic quality, assignment stability, and agreement
between current research and future-work statements.
None independently establishes the validity of
longitudinal research trends.

Several limitations constrain interpretation.
First, the analyzed ACL corpus covers 2012–2022
with uneven annual representation, including only
33 papers in 2015. Moreover, 29.18% of papers
lack future-work references, and missingness may
be systematic. Normalized prevalence does not
eliminate this potential selection bias or establish
generalizability beyond the analyzed corpus.

Second, reference provenance remains unverified,
and missing references may reflect either absent
future-work statements or incomplete extraction.
Differences in text length, cue-based filtering,
and citation-related artifacts may affect topic
assignments. Without human validation, topic
interpretations remain provisional.

title: What Git Does Not Record: Provenance Legibility in Two AI-Assisted Research Repositories
abstract: Publishers and funders increasingly ask authors to disclose how AI tools contributed to a piece of research. In computational work the repository is where an author or an auditor would look for the answer, and we ask what it can actually supply. We audit two single-investigator repositories by the same author in the same field, each carrying a different class of agent residue: a prescriptive trace of standing rule files and a narrative trace of a running agent scratchpad, in repositories of 466 and 103 commits. The two are legible in opposite ways. 85.6% of the lines ever committed to the prescriptive trace are visible at the current revision, and a standing rule states a conclusion and discards the episode behind it; the narrative trace records episodes and shows 21.8%. Counted by revision the gap is far smaller: 15 of the prescriptive trace's 41 revisions leave no visible line, against 18 of the narrative trace's 41. The Co-Authored-By trailer, the field an automated audit reads, is one of three AI trailer keys Project A carries and covers 66 of the 121 commits carrying any. In Project B it has low sensitivity against an explicit within-repository proxy: 39 commits revise a file maintained to hold an agent's working notes and 1 (2.6%) carries the trailer. Project A's repository-level rate is unstable in time too, stepping from 2.7% to 17.7% across a boundary we did not specify in advance. Repository channels disagree, and neither rate can be read as an involvement rate; we do not isolate the cause, and say so. We give a field-by-field account of which provenance claims such traces support, which they cannot, and which they answer confidently and wrongly, construct an auditable evidence ledger, and derive the requirements this places on any system meant to record research provenance as it happens.

Abstract

Publishers and funders increasingly ask authors to disclose how AI tools contributed to a
piece of research. In computational work the repository is where an author or an auditor
would look for the answer, and we ask what it can actually supply. We audit two single-investigator repositories by the same author in the same field, each carrying a different
class of agent residue: a prescriptive trace of standing rule files and a
narrative trace of a running agent scratchpad, in repositories of $466$ and $103$ 
commits. The two are
legible in opposite ways. $85.6\%$ of the lines ever committed to the prescriptive trace are
visible at the current revision, and a standing rule states a conclusion and discards the
episode behind it; the narrative trace records episodes and shows $21.8\%$ . Counted by
revision the gap is far smaller: $15$ of the prescriptive trace’s $41$ revisions leave no
visible line, against $18$ of the narrative trace’s $41$ . The Co-Authored-By trailer, the field
an automated audit reads, is one of three AI trailer keys Project A carries and covers $66$ of the
 $121$ commits carrying any. In Project B it has low sensitivity against an explicit
within-repository proxy: $39$ commits revise a file maintained to hold an agent’s working notes and $1$ 
( $2.6\%$ ) carries the trailer. Project A’s repository-level rate is unstable in time too,
stepping from $2.7\%$ to $17.7\%$ across a boundary we did not specify in advance. Repository
channels disagree, and neither rate can be read as an involvement rate; we do not isolate the
cause, and say so. We give a field-by-field account of which provenance claims such traces
support, which they cannot, and which they answer confidently and wrongly, construct an
auditable evidence ledger, and derive the requirements this places on any system meant to
record research provenance as it happens.

## 1 Introduction

The disclosure requirements now attached to AI use in research ask authors to describe
something that happened months earlier. Journals require a statement of how generative tools
contributed (Nature Editorial, 2023); conferences ask for the role LLMs played; reviewers,
when suspicious, ask for evidence. These policies specify where the statement goes, not
where its content is to come from. In computational research there is one obvious
candidate: the project’s version-control repository is already kept, timestamped, shared,
and treated as the authoritative record of how the work was built, and it is the first
place an author reconstructing their own process, or an auditor checking it, would look.
Whether it can carry that weight is an empirical question. A repository records a narrow
thing: a sequence of snapshots of a file tree, each annotated with a name, an email
address, two timestamps, and a free-text message, all supplied by the committer and none
verified. Projects using agentic coding tools commonly add one thing more, a persistent
artifact holding the agent’s standing instructions or its working notes between sessions.
Where such an artifact is tracked, it is the closest thing to a contemporaneous record of
AI involvement an ordinary repository contains, and it is what an auditor would read. The
two repositories we audit carry structurally different artifacts of this kind, and what
each presents to a reader is the subject of the paper. It is a comparison of two cases,
not a controlled manipulation, and we claim only what that licenses.

## Design.

We compare two repositories from a single investigator working in the environmental sciences
(Table 1). Project A ( $466$ commits) was developed with an agentic coding
assistant whose persistent artifact is a directory of standing rule files: instructions the
agent is to follow on future work. We call this a prescriptive trace. Project B ( $103$ 
commits) is a Cursor-assisted project, evidenced by a versioned agent scratchpad tracked
across $39$ commits; its artifact is a single running document of plans, findings and status,
rewritten as work proceeds. We call this a narrative trace. Author, discipline and
version-control substrate are shared; subject, period, commit volume, research phase and
how heavily each tool was used are not, and we manipulated none of them. Tool, artifact
class, project and time are confounded, so no difference we report can be attributed to the
tool alone. What the shared author buys is narrower and still worth having: it removes the
most obvious rival explanation for a difference in record-keeping, and it makes the
within-repository comparisons in Section 6 comparisons within one
person’s practice.

## Findings.

The two artifacts are legible in opposite ways, and the failures are
complementary. The prescriptive trace accumulates, keeping $85.6\%$ of its committed lines
at the current revision, but a standing rule records a conclusion rather than the episode
that produced it. The narrative trace records episodes and shows only $21.8\%$ : the rest
is in the object database, recoverable by walking the file’s history rather than by reading
its contents, which is the distinction that matters for an audit. So the artifact that
records the process does not show it, and the artifact that shows itself does not record
the process. Both figures presuppose the artifact was committed at all, a choice neither
tool prompts for and neither warns against. The commit log fares worse than either. The field
an automated audit reads, the Co-Authored-By trailer, is absent from $38$ of the
 $39$ Project B commits that revise the agent’s own scratchpad, and its rate within
Project A moves from $2.7\%$ to $17.7\%$ across a silent month we located by inspecting the
series rather than specifying in advance. Why, we cannot say: the author may simply
have used an agent more after the boundary, and neither repository records a tool-settings
history or which process authored a commit (Section 6). What survives
that uncertainty is the consequence for an auditor. A disclosure rate read off the commit
log is not an involvement rate, cannot be converted into one from repository evidence, and
is not stable enough within one project to compare against itself.

## Contributions.

1. 

A field-by-field taxonomy of what an ordinary Git repository can, cannot, and only
apparently records about the provenance of a change (Section 4),
separating fields that are unrecoverable from fields that are recoverable but misleading.

2. 

A legibility measurement over two AI-trace artifacts (Section 5):
what share of the lines ever committed to each is visible at the current revision, which
revisions survive into it, and how each artifact compares to every other tracked text file
in its own repository.

3. 

A measurement of the commit log’s disclosure channel (Section 6):
its sensitivity against an explicit within-repository proxy for agent activity, and the
instability of its rate over time, with the alternative explanations we cannot rule out.

4. 

Requirements for any system intending to capture research provenance in situ
(Section 8), derived field by field from the taxonomy’s gaps.

Our analysis produces an auditable ledger behind every number: one row per artifact revision,
disclosing commit, tracked text file and blame cohort.

## 2 Related work

## Provenance and the integrity of the record.

Formal provenance models specify
what a computational result must record to be accountable: entities, the activities that
produced them, and responsible agents (Moreau et al., 2011; Freire et al., 2008). The reproducibility literature consistently finds that this
record is not a by-product of ordinary practice and has to be deliberately produced
(Peng, 2011; Stodden et al., 2016; Pineau et al., 2021). Supply-chain work adds
cryptographic attestation and transparency logs on top of the repository
(Torres-Arias et al., 2019; Newman et al., 2022), binding an identity to an artifact but
presupposing that the events worth attesting were identified first. We measure that prior step: which provenance
fields survive in the Git repository of an AI-assisted project.

## Mining repositories.

Repository mining has long-standing cautions about
treating Git history as a faithful record of development: commits are curated, rebased,
squashed and back-dated, and repository metadata systematically misrepresents authorship
and effort (Bird et al., 2009; Kalliamvakou et al., 2016; Gousios and Spinellis, 2012).
We take the cautions as the object of study rather than as a threat to mitigate, and ask what
they imply for provenance claims about AI involvement.
The commit history of an AI-assisted research repository has also been mined for reusable
agent practice (Wu, 2026), and scientific code repositories have been turned into
environments that agents learn from (Geng et al., 2026). That work reads the repository
for what an agent can reuse, whereas we read it for what it can attest.

## AI disclosure and its verification.

Venue policies now require authors to declare AI use (Nature Editorial, 2023), and studies of
the resulting literature estimate rising LLM involvement from textual signal
(Liang et al., 2024).
Benchmarks of autonomous research find that agents still depend heavily on human
methodological guidance (Zhou et al., 2026).
Reasoning models trained with reinforcement learning can fail when the partial work they build
on contains misleading or corrupted steps, unless they are explicitly trained to detect and
repair such steps, for example through adversarial self-play
(Li et al., 2026). Scoring the end-to-end output of research agents
takes expert-written rubrics even under controlled conditions
(Xu et al., 2026). Research is therefore shared
between author and agent, and that division is what a disclosure has to describe.
Verification from the artifact is harder than it looks: generated
text is not reliably detectable post hoc (Sadasivan et al., 2025), watermarking requires
cooperation at generation time (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023), and integrity failures such
as fabricated references are recoverable only by checking the claim, not the process
(Walters and Wilder, 2023; Birhane et al., 2023). Closest to us, repository studies already
count AI self-declaration in the wild from commit messages and co-author trailers
(Kashif et al., 2026; Tufano et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026). They take the declaration
as the measurement; we ask what it can establish.

## Structured disclosure.

Datasheets and model cards established that useful
disclosure requires a fixed schema with named fields, including fields whose answer is “not
recorded” (Gebru et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2019), which
Section 8 applies to process provenance.

## 3 Method

## 3.1 Unit of analysis

The unit of analysis is the AI-trace artifact: the file or directory an agentic tool
maintains in the repository to carry state between sessions. Taking the artifact rather than
the project as the unit is what makes the two repositories comparable, since their research
content is not, and the trace is what an auditor would read. Table 1 states the
two cases and its caption what they share, as a description rather than a design matrix.

Project B’s AI involvement is stated exactly as we can evidence it and no further: it is a
Cursor-assisted project, evidenced by a versioned agent scratchpad tracked across $39$ 
commits. We do not claim a proportion of the code was model-written, because nothing in the
repository would support such a claim, and the inability to support it is part of our
result.

One premise deserves stating, because a later result rests on it. The file at
.cursor/scratchpad.md is a project convention, not a format the tool creates and
maintains on its own: it lives in the tool’s configuration directory, holds plans, findings
and running status in the tool’s working idiom, and the project kept it under version
control. We treat revisions to it as a proxy for contemporaneous agent activity, imperfect
in both directions: a human can edit the file directly, and an agent session can produce
work committed later, separately, or alongside unrelated changes. Every claim in Section 6 that rests on it is marked as such.

## 3.2 Measurement

Four scripts run over both repositories, a fifth turns their output into every coordinate

union of the paths it has occupied, and record per-revision insertions and deletions; count
the lines the census revision still shows; check whether the artifact is git-ignored;
extract commit-message trailers; and compare dates the artifact asserts about itself against
the commit that introduced each line. Three measurement decisions are worth
stating, because the naive alternatives give indefensible numbers.

First, the query decides part of the answer. Project A’s trace directory was

abstract: The CIDOC CRM family is not only a schema for museum collections. Its extensions formalise the apparatus through which research knowledge is produced and justified: CRMsci models scientific observation and measurement, CRMdig the provenance of digital processes, CRMinf inference and belief. Together they constitute a schema for research data, and the obstacle to their adoption is documentary rather than theoretical: four normative documents, four code conventions, and eighty-nine typed links crossing document boundaries. This paper presents the CIDOC CRM Periodic Table, a single-page browser rendering 131 classes and 480 property entries from CIDOC CRM 7.1.3, CRMsci 3.2, CRMdig 5.0 and CRMinf 1.2.1 as one navigable surface, with two inference facilities: a one-step triple builder admitting only the class-property combinations licensed by declared domains, ranges and the subclass closure, and a multi-step path finder enumerating property chains between two classes. Because all loaded models are merged into one code-keyed dictionary before the hierarchy closures are computed, both resolve chains that cross model boundaries; we document the addition of CRMsci and the three cross-model tests it made possible, and report preliminary uptake signals from 56 months of analytics, with the reading they support.

## 1 Introduction

A standard is adopted through its documentation, and a standard that grows by
extension fragments its documentation along the same seams: what a modeller needs to
know ends up distributed across the very modules that make the standard extensible.
The CIDOC Conceptual Reference Model Bekiari et al. (2024), standardised as ISO 21127, is
accompanied by a family of extensions that, taken together, describe how
empirical claims come to be: CRMsci Doerr et al. (2026b) defines itself as “a global
schema for integrating metadata about scientific observation, measurements and
processed data in descriptive and empirical sciences such as life sciences,
geology, geography, archaeology, cultural heritage conservation and others in
research IT environments and research data libraries”; CRMdig Doerr et al. (2025)
models the provenance of digital processes; CRMinf Doerr et al. (2026a) models
inference, argumentation and belief. A researcher who wants to say what was
observed, by which instrument, through which digital transformation, and on what
grounds the resulting statement is believed, already has a normative vocabulary
for all four moves.

What that researcher does not have is a workable way to read it. Nine years ago,
in a peer-reviewed venue, Guillem and Bruseker argued that CIDOC CRM adoption in
concrete practice is limited because ontologies are “considered too complicated
and abstract for application in real life scenarios” Guillem and Bruseker (2017).
Since then the specification has grown rather than shrunk. Covering the four
models discussed here means reading four separate documents that declare 131
classes and 480 property entries, use four disjoint code conventions
(E/P, S/O, D/L,
I/J), and connect to each other through 89 subClassOf
and subPropertyOf declarations that point out of the document one is
currently reading. The barrier is documentary, and it grows with every extension the
family gains.

## 2 Background: the CRM family as research-data infrastructure

Read individually, each extension looks like a specialist concern. Read together,
they cover the lifecycle of an empirical claim. Take a mundane research workflow:
a sample is taken, it is measured with an instrument, the instrument writes a file,
and someone draws a conclusion. Every step is already declared, across three of the
four models: S2 Sample Taking -O5 removed-> S13 Sample;
S21 Measurement -O24 measured-> S13, admissible because S13
descends from S15 Observable Entity, the declared range, with
S21 -O39 observed dimension-> E54 Dimension for the value;
D11 Digital Measurement Event $\sqsubseteq$ S21, CRMdig
subclassing CRMsci, with D11 -L20 has created-> D9 Data Object; and
S5 Inference Making $\sqsubseteq$ I1 Argumentation, CRMsci
subclassing CRMinf, with I1 -J2 concluded that-> I2 Belief. This is a
schema for research data, not for catalogue records, which is what Beretta’s SDHSS
ecosystem argues from the side of the social sciences and
humanities Beretta (2024). Its provenance half overlaps with what
PROV-O Lebo et al. (2013) models generically; CRMdig differs in committing to the same
event-centric ontology as the observation and inference halves — which is
precisely why the four documents have to be read together.

The decisive point for tooling is that these models are interlocked, not
parallel: they are not four self-contained documents, each readable on its own, but
documents that declare entities whose superclass or superproperty is defined in another
one. S5 Inference Making is declared a subclass of CRMinf’s
I1 Argumentation; S27 Observation likewise; CRMdig’s
D11 Digital Measurement Event is a subclass of CRMsci’s
S21 Measurement, and L1 digitized a subproperty of CRMsci’s
O24 measured. Counting from the machine-readable releases, the four
models declare 89 links whose target lives in a different document
(Appendix A): 31 from CRMdig, 30 from CRMsci and 28 from CRMinf.
Ten of CRMsci’s point at CRMinf rather than at base CRM, and three of CRMdig’s
point at CRMsci.

The practical consequence is that reading one specification is never enough, and
the workflow above shows it concretely. A modeller who opens CRMdig alone sees that
D11 creates a D9, and misses that D11 is a
measurement and therefore already carries O24 measured and
O39 observed dimension; a modeller who opens CRMsci alone cannot see that
the properties of I1 Argumentation apply to S5. The official HTML
declarations, published per model and per version, faithfully mirror the documents
— and therefore mirror the fragmentation too. This is the gap the interface
targets, and it is a documentation problem of the kind the community meets whenever
scholarly knowledge is represented in a modular standard: comparable
infrastructures for scholarly knowledge, such as the Open Research Knowledge
Graph Jaradeh et al. (2019), invest heavily in making their model legible to
contributors for the same reason.

## 3 Related work

Three genres of resource already address parts of this problem, and it is worth
being precise about which part (Table 1).

Specification renderings are faithful to their input and inherit its
boundaries: the CRM-SIG’s machine-generated declarations give one HTML page per model
per version, and generated documentation such as WIDOCO Garijo (2017) or
visualisers such as WebVOWL Lohmann et al. (2015) do the same for arbitrary
vocabularies. In all of them a reference into another model stays a string.

Ontology management. OntoME is the closest neighbour — a collaborative
environment handling multiple namespaces, profiles and versioning, which lets users
align their own classes to CIDOC CRM and compatible models Beretta (2021)
and does resolve the family as one graph. Its centre of gravity is authoring and
curation, one page per entity; ours is reading a whole model at once and testing
what it licenses.

General-purpose tooling. One can load all four RDFS files into an editor such
as Protégé Musen (2015) with an OWL reasoner behind it, and in terms of
raw capability that suffices. The difference is one of purpose. An editor supports
building and verifying an ontology: its unit of work is the axiom, its
question whether a model is consistent. The task here is downstream and far more
common — applying a standardised ontology one did not design, translating
“this sample was measured, and here is the file the instrument wrote” into its
codes. An editor supplies the vocabulary but no help in choosing within it, and
asking “which properties may hold between a sample and a data object” costs a
reasoning environment and a formalised query; here it costs a URL. Documentation and
modelling support are usually separate artefacts; for a modular standard they should
not be.

Three neighbours sit outside the table. Mountantonakis et al. catalogue which
datasets use which classes and properties Mountantonakis et al. (2023):
instance-level evidence, where we offer schema-level navigation. Linked Art narrows
the model instead, publishing a profile over a subset of CIDOC CRM
7.1.3 Linked Art Editorial Board (2024) — a subset helps the modeller who accepts its scope,
navigation helps the one who cannot. Closest in spirit at this workshop, Tietz et
al. treat cultural-heritage material as research data and build discovery services
over it Tietz et al. (2025): the same premise, applied to the data rather than the
schema. Tools we could not verify are deliberately not cited.

## 4 Design

The interface renders every class of every enabled model as a cell on a single
scrolling page, and every property as a line in a companion view
(Figure 2 schematises that surface and
Figure 3 shows one block of it as rendered). Four decisions do
most of the work.

Placement follows the code. A cell’s code prefix determines
which model it belongs to and whether it is a class or a property; the four code
spaces are disjoint, so a code denotes exactly one entry across the loaded family.
Cells then flow inline and wrap, so the grid reflows to the width available instead
of being pinned to fixed columns. Each model occupies one contiguous block, introduced by a
full-width header in the model’s own hue, so provenance is legible without a
legend.

Colour is inherited through the hierarchy. Seven anchor classes —
E4 Temporal Entity, E18 Physical Thing, E39 Actor,
E28 Conceptual Object, E41 Appellation, E53 Place,
E55 Type — define seven colour families, and every class takes the colour
of the anchor it descends from through the subClassOf closure. Nothing is
hard-coded per class, so adding a model costs no colour work: 20 of CRMsci’s 28
classes were coloured as intended the moment they were loaded. Grouping CRM’s classes
into colour-coded families is not our idea: we inherit it, along with the association
between family and hue, from the CIDOC CRM Game Guillem and Bruseker (2017); Bruseker et al. (2021).
The anchors, the values, the derivation of colour by inheritance, and the second
colour axis marking which model an entry comes from are ours; no graphic material
from the game was reused.

Inheritance depth is legible on the cell. Each cell carries the codes of its
immediate superclasses and a marker that shrinks with the length of its longest
inheritance path, separating E1 from a class eight steps below it.

The URL carries the state. The query string of the browser URL —
?ont=crm,crmsci, ?code=S4, ?path=S13,D9 — is read on load
and rewritten on interaction, so any class, filter combination or path query is a
citable link, and a deep link silently enables the model that owns its entry. These are
view parameters and not identifiers: an entity’s URI remains the one its ontology
declares, carried on the cell and on the copy action, though it deserves to be shown in
the detail panel too.

Accommodating CRMsci exercised exactly these mechanisms. It uses S for
classes and O for properties, a convention shared with neither base CRM nor
the other extensions, so it needed a registry entry, two code-prefix declarations, a
data file and a provenance hue — and nothing else. The hue was chosen by measurement
rather than taste: indigo (#3A3FA0) sits 37 degrees of hue from its nearest
neighbour among the two model hues and the seven family colours, at 8.8:1 contrast on
white.

## 5 Inference support

A documentation browser is easy to build; letting a modeller assemble a triple and
see what the specification licenses is the distinctive part, and the place where
over-claiming is most tempting, so we state the boundaries plainly.

One step. The user picks a domain class, a property and a range class in
any order, and the table dims every entry that the choice has excluded. The rule is
subsumption over declared domains and ranges: a class is admissible in a slot if it
is the declared domain or range of the property, or a subclass of it through the
transitive subClassOf closure; a property is admissible if the classes
already chosen fall within its declared domain and range in the same sense. The
completed triple is read back as an English sentence and as parsable Turtle. The
Turtle is built at instance level, with blank nodes and only the @prefix
declarations the triple actually uses, because CRM properties hold between instances
and a triple asserted between classes would be meaningless.

Multiple steps. The path finder takes two classes and enumerates property
chains between them, using a bounded bidirectional breadth-first search over the
domain/range graph, with subsumption applied at every hop: a property is available
on a class if the class or any of its superclasses is the declared domain. Results
are grouped by chain length and ranked by the specificity of the properties
involved. The bounds are what make this tractable: each side expands at most half the
requested depth, every level is beam-limited to its 600 most specific states and the
answer set to 100, so the work per query grows with those caps and the branching of the
domain/range graph rather than exponentially with depth, and any truncation is reported
on screen. The search runs synchronously in the browser over the whole loaded family;
it is the caps, not the size of the family, that keep it interactive. An optional loose mode admits hops that are valid only if the
intermediate instance belongs to a more specific class than the chain guarantees —
the downcasts that are common in real modelling — and such chains are dashed and
labelled in the output, never silently mixed with sound ones
(Figure 1).

Cross-model chains are structural. Every loaded model is merged into one
dictionary keyed by bare code, and the subclass and subproperty closures are
computed after the merge, over the union. Nothing in the search knows about
namespaces; a chain crosses a model boundary the same way it crosses any other
edge. The CRMsci import let us test this on the three cases that exist in the
data; each is a deep link, so each is re-enterable
(?ont=crm,crminf,crmdig,crmsci&path=). First, CRMsci to base CRM:
S4,E53 yields 11 sound chains within two steps, five of them touching
three models. Second, CRMsci to CRMinf: S5,I2 yields exactly one sound
chain, S5 -J2-> I2, and it exists only because S5 Inference
Making inherits the domain of a CRMinf property through
S5 $\sqsubseteq$ I1 Argumentation. This is the case a reader of CRMsci
alone cannot see, and it is the example we would put in front of a sceptic. Third,
CRMdig to CRMsci, D11,S13: before the import, D11’s superclass
S21 was an inert label and no chain could pass through it; after it,

limitations:
The tool has never been evaluated with users, and the analytics above are not a
substitute. Coverage of the family is partial: CRMgeo, CRMarchaeo and CRMba are
not loaded, and references into them remain inert labels. The inference
facilities cover the fragment described in Section 5 and no
more. There is no automated test suite. Two interface decisions belong here as well.
The layout assumes a desktop viewport: the premise of the tool is a whole model in view
at once, which is desk work, and it does not lay out for small screens. And the colour
families, derived and documented in Section 4, have no legend in the
interface itself — the per-model chips double as one for provenance, the seven family
hues have no equivalent.

How far this generalises. Within the CRM family the answer is settled by
construction: a further model costs a registry entry, its code prefixes, a data file and
a hue, as CRMsci did; models with two-letter prefixes — CRMgeo’s SP,
CRMarchaeo’s AP — additionally need the code pattern widened, a contained
change. Beyond the family the boundary is not in the code but in an assumption about the
domain. The table rests on a convention that is universal in the CRM family and general
nowhere: that every class and property carries a short mnemonic code of one letter and a
number. That code decides the cell, the owning model and the class/property split — and
it is declared nowhere in the RDF, there being no property that states it, so it is
recovered heuristically from the local name of the URI. A vocabulary without such codes
could still have the cross-document closure, the constrained triple builder and the path
finder, which need only RDFS; it could not have the periodic table. We would therefore
claim generalisation to modular, code-bearing standards, and no further.

The roadmap follows from that list, in order of what would change most: a teaching
study in a graduate course, where the tool is already being used informally;
systematic verification of the implemented entailments against the normative
declarations, beginning with subPropertyOf; the remaining
compatible extensions, for which the CRMsci import is now the template; and two small
debts to the reader, a legend for the colour families and the entity URI shown in the
detail panel.
conclusion:
The CIDOC CRM family already offers a normative vocabulary for observation, digital
provenance and inference — for the apparatus by which research data is produced and
justified. What it does not offer is a way to read four interlocking documents at
once and check what they license together, and that gap is not a detail of
presentation: it is where the cost of adopting the standard is actually paid.

The Periodic Table takes the modest position that this is a tooling problem rather
than a modelling one. Its design result is small enough to state in a sentence —
merge every loaded model into one dictionary keyed by bare code, then compute the
hierarchy closures over the union — and its consequence is that cross-model
inspection stops being a special case and becomes the default. Adding CRMsci
exercised precisely that: a registry entry, two code prefixes, a data file and a
colour, after which chains cut at the document boundary resolved on their own, and
the same four steps — with the code pattern widened where a model’s prefixes run
to two letters — are what it would take to bring in CRMgeo, CRMarchaeo or CRMba.

Two limits travel with the claim. The inference facilities implement a fragment —
subclass transitivity and domain/range applicability — and we say which entailments
are absent, because a tool that answers “what may I say about this?” is trusted, and
trust must not be borrowed against. And it has never been evaluated with users: 56
months of traffic establish that people reach it, not that it helps them. What we would draw from this is more general than CIDOC CRM: modular standards
distribute their meaning across documents and leave the reader to recompose it; where
that recomposition is mechanical, the documentation can perform it.

Abstract

Generative AI’s growing role in academic writing has driven a rise in fabricated references across dissertations and student reports. We present the Fabrication Severity Stack (FSS), a three-tiered framework classifying citation fabrications by detection complexity - from non-existent references to subtle content misattribution.
Building on the FSS, we propose a staged heuristic verification workflow, executable through mainstream LLM interfaces. We argue that this framework offers computer science educators/examiners a practical, zero-cost basis for embedding reference verification into the assessment of dissertation and students’ reports. In a pilot study on 100 citations (20% seeded with Level 1 and Level 2 fabrications), the proposed heuristic workflow enabled mainstream LLM interfaces to correctly flag 9–10 of 10 non-existent references and partially detect metadata corruption. These preliminary results suggest that freely accessible, general-purpose LLMs can achieve high recall on citation verification without reliance on proprietary detection tools.

## 1 Fabrication Severity Stack

Citation of relevant literature lies at the core of academic scholarship and students’ writing, serving as the foundation for validating claims and anchoring discoveries. However, as Generative AI increasingly becomes a ubiquitous tool in academic writing, a critical vulnerability has emerged: the proliferation of “fabricated citations” within dissertations, student reports, and beyond. Dissertations and reports are increasingly being authored with LLM assistance, specifically during literature review and related-work drafting – precisely the stages most susceptible to fabricated citations. Hence, computer science educators/examiners who evaluate these documents therefore need a systematic vocabulary and a repeatable verification procedure, rather than relying on spot-checks or intuition.

Independent audits corroborate the scale of the problem. For example, a systematic comparison of ChatGPT-generated bibliographies found that a substantial share of references were either entirely non-existent or contained material citation errors such as incorrect authorship, wrong publication years, or fabricated DOIs [4]. Even peer-reviewed venues are not immune. An analysis by Topaz et al. found more than 4,000 fabricated references in studies published betweeen Jan 2023 and Feb 2026 [3]. An audit of ACL Anthology papers documented a rise in hallucinated references between 2024 and 2025 [2]. Of 700,000 citations in submissions made to ICLR 202611
 1

 International Conference on Learning Representations, GPTZero flagged 9,000 citations that required additional manual checking [1].

In this context, this work categorizes AI-generated reference fabrications into a three-layered hierarchy based on the complexity and severity of their detection. We conceptualize this taxonomy as the Fabrication Severity Stack (FSS), a structured framework for analysing and understanding fabricated citations in computer science dissertations, students’ reports, and beyond.
The FSS-based categorization consists of the following three levels:

Level 1 – Syntactic Non-Existence. Total fabrication or absolute LLM hallucinations of titles, DOIs, or papers that do not exist at all. These are often easily identifiable via automated metadata lookups, DOI verification (e.g., on Crossref), and direct web searches.

Level 2 – Metadata Corruption. Partial hallucinations where valid metadata elements are blended with fabricated ones. Their detection might pose a medium-complexity challenge and require cross-referencing multiple metadata fields to flag inconsistencies.

Level 3 – Content Corruption. The paper exists, and all metadata is perfectly valid, but the cited text does not support the author’s claim (e.g., fabricated / selective quotation, or misattributed findings). Detection of such cases might be highly complex and often requires full-text retrieval, semantic analysis, or advanced RAG-based tools.

Figure 1: A heuristics-based verification workflow.

## 2 Heuristic-Based Workflow

We outline a lightweight, three-stage pipeline that computer science educators can execute manually or semi-automate with a general-purpose LLM interface, without requiring a bespoke detection tool (also see Fig. 1):

• 

Existence Check. For each reference, resolve the DOI or URL against an authoritative indexer (Crossref, DBLP, arXiv, PubMed, or Google Scholar). A reference is flagged immediately if the DOI does not resolve, the URL returns a dead link, or no matching record can be located under any permutation of the stated title. This single check disposes of the majority of total fabrications.

Sample Prompt

For every citation below, determine whether it corresponds to a real, locatable publication. Attempt to resolve the DOI/URL if present, and
search Crossref, DBLP, arXiv, PubMed, or Google Scholar for the title under reasonable variations (typos, subtitle differences, translated
titles). Output one of: EXISTS (with source + link), NOT FOUND. If EXISTS, note whether
the found record matches the title exactly or only approximately.

• 

Metadata Consistency Check. For references that pass the existence check, cross-validate author list, publication year, venue, and volume/page numbers against the indexer record. The aim is to identify specific metadata discrepancies, for example; a real paper title attached to the wrong author list, or a plausible-sounding venue that never published the cited study. Automating these checks thus reveals metadata blending and warrants closer inspection.

Sample Prompt

For every citation below, check the fields (authors, year, venue, volume, pages) and output MATCH, MISMATCH, or PARTIAL per field, plus
a one-line reason for any non-match. Do not judge the paper’s content.
Output as a single table with columns:

Reference — Field — Status — Reason

• 

Claim-Support Check. For references surviving the first two stages, sample a subset of citations (prioritizing those supporting the dissertation’s central claims) and retrieve the actual cited passage or abstract. An LLM, or the examiner, then assesses whether the passage substantiates the specific claim attributed to it, distinguishing genuine support from selective quotation, overgeneralization, or outright misattribution. Because this stage requires semantic judgment rather than lookup, it is relatively labor-intensive and should be applied selectively rather than exhaustively.

Preliminary results:
To assess the practical viability of the proposed heuristic workflow, we conducted an initial pilot study on a curated set of 100 citations drawn from student dissertation bibliographies, of which 20 (20%) were deliberately seeded with fabrications spanning Level 1 (non-existent references) and Level 2 (metadata-corrupted references) of the FSS, in equal proportion. Two mainstream LLM interfaces, Claude, Sonnet 5 and Gemini, Flash 3.5, were evaluated using the existence-check and metadata-consistency prompts described above. Claude correctly flagged all 10 Level 1 fabrications, and additionally surfaced several Level 2 cases by identifying mismatched author lists and blended metadata fields, indicating that a single structured pass can partially generalize beyond its targeted severity tier. Gemini correctly flagged 9 of the 10 Level 1 fabrications, missing one case where the fabricated title closely resembled a real publication. While this pilot is small in scale and does not yet constitute a large scale benchmark, it suggests that mainstream, freely accessible LLM interfaces — without bespoke detection infrastructure — can achieve high recall on citation verification, lending preliminary support to the idea that expensive proprietary tools may not be a strict prerequisite for effective citation screening.

## 3 Final Remarks

Rigorous citation verification has become an indispensable component in assessments. The rapid evolution of LLM technology has led to growth in specialized detection tools.22
 2

 Examples include: GPTZero, SwanRef, CiteTrue, CiteMe, Citely, CiteCheck, CiteSure, and MisciteBench. More updates on https://github.com/anonymized/anonymized.. Academics might not need to rely on expensive detection tools, as comparable outcomes can be achieved by employing structured heuristic workflows via mainstream LLM interfaces. This approach centers on automating the verification of citations for: (i) DOI/URL validity, (ii) title/author consistency, and (iii) metadata alignment across indexers (PubMed/arXiv/Scholar). References failing any of these automated or semi-automated checks should be flagged for manual review rather than automatically rejected, since indexer coverage gaps and formatting idiosyncrasies can produce false positives. Applying stages (i) and (ii) across an entire bibliography is inexpensive and should be treated as a crucial pre-submission step for dissertations and theses, analogous to running a plagiarism check. Stage (iii), by contrast, is best reserved for spot-checking claims, since Level 3 fabrications are structurally distinct from Levels 1 and 2 (the reference itself is entirely legitimate) and consequently present a substantially greater diagnostic challenge that current automated tools handle unreliably [2]. We acknowledge the preliminary nature and limited scale of the pilot study.

title: First Passage Attention
abstract: Augmenting softmax attention with forget gates typically relies on summing decay contributions along the key--query path. Because such accumulation is monotonic, these mechanisms cannot selectively erase intermediate context while preserving older, structurally relevant tokens. We propose First Passage Attention (FPA), which shifts from path summation to path extrema by lowering a key's logit proportionally to the deepest dip of a learned scalar field below that key's level over the intervening span. FPA encompasses the Forgetting Transformer (FoX) as a special case, and when the field and levels follow a shared learned walk, the alive keys with unpenalised logits naturally form a stack.
